messages.content: I want to determine whether population treatment-policy effects are identifiable under network interference when treatment influences which social ties are observed. The goal is to establish identification boundaries under explicit restrictions on interference and treatment-dependent missing ties. In regimes where identification is possible, I also want 95% intervals with at least 93% coverage and median width no more than 2× that of a complete-network oracle.

That poses two distinct questions. First, under what explicitly stated restrictions can the population treatment-policy effects be determined from the available information, despite network interference and treatment-dependent observation of ties? Second, within the regimes found to be identifiable, can 95% intervals meet both performance targets: coverage of at least 93% and median width at most 2× the complete-network oracle’s?
Why does treatment affecting which ties are observed matter for identification?

With network interference, an individual’s outcome may depend on treatment beyond their own treatment, through social connections. If treatment also influences which of those connections are observed, the recorded network may not reveal all the ties relevant to that dependence. Identifiability then cannot be assessed solely by treating the observed ties as though they were necessarily the complete network. This describes the obstacle, not a conclusion that identification always fails.
So the issue is not just missing ties in general, but missing ties whose observation depends on treatment?

Yes. The stated setting specifically involves treatment-dependent missing ties: treatment influences which social ties are observed. That matters alongside interference because ties may be relevant to how treatment relates to outcomes across a network. The goal is to say precisely what can and cannot be identified under explicit restrictions on both interference and that observation process.
Does saying treatment influences observed ties mean treatment necessarily changes the underlying social network?

No. Influencing which ties are observed does not, by itself, establish whether the underlying ties change. The identification question concerns what can be learned when the available view of social ties depends on treatment. It should not be recast as a claim about changes to the underlying network without further information.
What would it mean to establish an identification boundary here?

It would mean making the relevant restrictions explicit and distinguishing regimes in which the population treatment-policy effects are identifiable from regimes in which the available information does not identify them. A boundary should explain how the conclusion depends on restrictions on interference and treatment-dependent missing ties, rather than making an unqualified claim that the effects are identifiable or nonidentifiable in every setting.
Are any particular interference restrictions or rules for missing ties already specified?

Not in the goal as stated. It calls for explicit restrictions, but it does not give their precise form. Naming a particular restriction now as though it were part of the setting would add a task-specific assumption. The identification conclusions will need to be stated conditionally on whatever restrictions are actually established.
I want the population treatment-policy part to remain central, rather than turning this into a question about a single person’s treatment effect.

Agreed. The target is the effect of a treatment policy at the population level in the presence of network interference. A discussion of observed and unobserved ties is relevant because it bears on whether that target can be identified; it does not replace the target with an individual-level effect. No particular treatment policy or policy contrast is specified here, so those details should remain open.
How do the interval targets relate to the identification boundaries?

The interval targets apply within identifiable regimes. Establishing identification boundaries comes first conceptually: it indicates where inference about the population treatment-policy effects is supported under the stated restrictions. In those regimes, the requested performance is at least 93% coverage for 95% intervals, while keeping median interval width at or below 2× the complete-network oracle’s. Those are goals, not results already demonstrated.
Is at least 93% coverage the same thing as requiring the 95% intervals to attain exactly 95% coverage?

No. The intervals are described as 95% intervals, and the stated performance threshold is coverage of at least 93%. The two numbers serve different roles: 95% names the intervals’ nominal level, while 93% is the minimum coverage target specified here. The goal does not assert that any intervals have already attained either figure.
And what is the comparison in the width requirement?

The comparison is to a complete-network oracle. Within identifiable regimes, the target is a median interval width no more than 2× the oracle’s. That benchmark keeps track of the precision cost relative to an oracle with the complete network; it does not imply that the complete network is observed in the setting under study.
Could narrow intervals alone satisfy the goal?

No. The width limit and the coverage threshold are joint requirements within identifiable regimes. Intervals whose median width meets the 2× oracle limit would still fall short of the stated goal if their coverage for 95% intervals were below 93%. Likewise, meeting the coverage threshold would not by itself satisfy the width requirement.
Could we apply those numerical targets to regimes where the effects are not identified?

That would go beyond the stated objective. The numerical targets are expressly scoped to identifiable regimes. For a regime where the population treatment-policy effect is not identified under the applicable restrictions, the relevant conclusion is about the identification boundary; the goal does not ask the intervals to overcome that lack of identification.
Then the full question is conditional: identify the boundaries under explicit restrictions, and assess interval performance only on the identifiable side of those boundaries?

Exactly. The question is whether population treatment-policy effects can be identified under network interference when treatment influences which social ties are observed, and where the answer changes under explicit restrictions on interference and treatment-dependent missing ties. Within the identifiable regimes, the separate performance target is ≥93% coverage for 95% intervals and median width ≤2× that of the complete-network oracle. Neither the identification conclusions nor attainment of those numerical targets is assumed in advance.

For the identification question, I’d like to consider a proposal under randomized assignment, one-hop interference, and positive treatment-stratified dyad audits: use policy g-computation with cluster-bootstrap intervals and MNAR bounds.

That is a conditional proposal, not an identification result yet. Randomized assignment addresses how treatment is allocated; one-hop interference restricts how far treatment effects can propagate through social ties; and positive treatment-stratified dyad audits provide an opportunity to learn about ties across the relevant treatment strata. Policy g-computation would be the proposed way to evaluate population treatment-policy effects, cluster-bootstrap intervals the proposed uncertainty procedure, and MNAR bounds a way to address remaining uncertainty about ties that are missing not at random.
Why emphasize randomized assignment if treatment can still influence which ties we observe?

Because those are different processes. Randomized assignment specifies how treatment is assigned; it does not, by itself, make observation of social ties independent of treatment. The proposal retains treatment-dependent tie observation as an issue to address through the audits and, where needed, MNAR bounds.
What does the one-hop restriction contribute?

It limits the interference under consideration to treatment acting through a person’s direct social ties, rather than through arbitrarily long paths in the network. That narrows the network information relevant to the proposed policy analysis. It does not mean direct ties are all observed, nor does it eliminate the problem when treatment affects which direct ties appear in the data.
Would it be accurate to say one-hop interference rules out any role for other people’s treatment?

No. Direct neighbors’ treatment can still matter under one-hop interference. The restriction concerns the reach of interference, not a return to an assumption that only a person’s own treatment matters. It also does not specify the exact form of the dependence on neighbors’ treatment.
Explain the positive treatment-stratified dyad audits without assuming they magically recover the whole network.

The positivity condition means dyads have a nonzero opportunity to be audited in the treatment strata relevant to the proposal. Stratifying audits by treatment is pertinent because treatment influences which ties are observed. An audited subset can provide information that would not be available from the observed network alone, but positive auditing does not mean every dyad is audited or that the complete network becomes observed. Exactly what the audits identify still depends on what they reveal and the restrictions used to connect audited and unaudited dyads.
So even with randomized treatment and positive audits, we shouldn’t simply announce point identification?

Right. Those conditions are components of a proposed route to identification, not a blanket guarantee. The identification boundary still needs to be established under explicit restrictions on interference and treatment-dependent missing ties. If the information and restrictions do not determine a unique population treatment-policy effect, the proposal’s MNAR-bounds component is relevant rather than presenting a point value as identified.
What is policy g-computation doing in this proposal?

Conceptually, it uses relationships supported by the available data and the stated assumptions to calculate outcomes under a treatment policy and aggregate them to the population level. With one-hop interference, those calculations must account for treatment in the relevant direct-tie neighborhood, not just each person’s own treatment. Because observed ties can depend on treatment, the calculation also needs an appropriate account of the tie information; merely plugging in the recorded network as if it were complete would skip the central difficulty.
Do we have to specify a particular policy or a particular outcome model in this fragment?

No particular policy, policy contrast, or outcome model is specified in the proposal. The method can be described at the level of policy g-computation without inventing those details. Any concrete identification or performance claim would have to be tied to the details and assumptions actually supplied when the analysis is made specific.
How do cluster-bootstrap intervals fit alongside g-computation?

They are the proposed interval procedure for estimates obtained through the policy analysis. In general, a cluster bootstrap resamples at the cluster level to account for dependence within clusters, rather than treating every observation as independent. The proposal does not define the clusters or establish that a particular bootstrap implementation is valid here, so its interval performance should remain a target to assess, not a presumed consequence of choosing a cluster bootstrap.
And the MNAR bounds—are they meant to say that treatment-dependent missing ties are always MNAR?

No. Treatment-dependent observation and missing not at random are not interchangeable claims. The proposal includes MNAR bounds to address the possibility that missing-tie behavior relevant to the effect cannot be resolved by treating the observed ties as representative. Without specified assumptions or a bounding construction, we should not assert a particular bound, its width, or whether it yields point identification.
Can g-computation, intervals, and bounds all be part of one coherent proposal?

Yes, provided their roles remain distinct. Policy g-computation concerns evaluation of population treatment-policy effects under the stated restrictions. Cluster-bootstrap intervals concern uncertainty for estimates in regimes where the target is identified and the interval procedure is justified. MNAR bounds concern what can be said when uncertainty about missing ties limits point identification. Calling them parts of one proposal does not establish that one procedure alone solves every regime.
Where does the complete-network oracle comparison enter?

It remains the precision benchmark from the goal. Within identifiable regimes, the desired performance is at least 93% coverage for 95% intervals and median width at most 2× the complete-network oracle’s. The proposed cluster-bootstrap intervals could be evaluated against those criteria, but the proposal supplies no result showing that either threshold has been met.
I also want to be careful that bounds aren’t reported as if they were ordinary 95% intervals around an identified effect.

That distinction matters. MNAR bounds express the range allowed by stated restrictions when the effect is not pinned down to a single value; sampling uncertainty about estimated bounds is a separate issue. The requirement concerning 95% intervals, ≥93% coverage, and median width ≤2× the complete-network oracle is explicitly for identifiable regimes. The proposal does not license treating a bound on a nonidentified effect as though it were an interval estimate with that same interpretation.
Then state the proposal in one sentence without suggesting it has already worked.

Under randomized assignment, one-hop interference, and positive treatment-stratified dyad audits, propose policy g-computation for population treatment-policy effects, cluster-bootstrap intervals in identifiable regimes, and MNAR bounds where uncertainty from treatment-dependent missing ties remains; identification and the interval-performance targets still have to be established.
Can positive dyad audits identify one-hop exposure distributions when treatment-dependent reporting also depends on unobserved tie status?

Positivity of dyad auditing is potentially useful, but it does not, on its own, settle identification. If whether a tie is reported depends both on treatment and on the tie’s true, otherwise unobserved status, the reported network can be selectively missing ties even within treatment strata. The key question is what the audits actually reveal and whether their selection permits audited dyads to inform the unobserved ones. Identifying a one-hop exposure distribution may also require information about how ties occur together around individuals, not merely whether individual dyads tend to be ties.
Why doesn’t stratifying the audits by treatment take care of reporting that depends on treatment?

Stratification addresses differences across the treatment strata covered by the audits. It does not automatically address selection within a stratum according to true tie status. If actual ties and non-ties have different chances of being reported even at the same treatment values, conditioning on treatment alone need not make the reported dyads representative of all dyads in that stratum.
But the audits have positive probability. Isn’t that the needed overlap?

It is an important overlap condition: relevant dyads must have a nonzero chance to be audited. Yet a nonzero chance is not a complete description of the audit process or of what is learned when an audit occurs. Positivity alone does not say that an audit reveals true tie status, that selection into auditing is adequately characterized, or that the audited information is rich enough for the particular one-hop exposure distribution.
Suppose, as a hypothetical, an audit verifies whether the dyad is truly tied. Would that make reporting based on unobserved tie status irrelevant?

Not necessarily irrelevant, but potentially addressable. If verified tie status is available for an appropriately selected audited subset, the audits could reveal how reporting differs between true ties and true non-ties within treatment strata. That could help account for tie-status-dependent reporting rather than assuming it away. Whether it identifies the desired exposure distribution still depends on how the audits relate to the full set of relevant dyads and on what aspects of the network the exposure requires.
So a positive chance of audit is different from an audit that reliably measures the underlying tie?

Exactly. The first is about the opportunity to be audited; the second is about the information an audit supplies. The proposal mentions positive treatment-stratified dyad audits but does not specify their measurement properties. An identification claim would need to keep those distinct.
Can you explain the difference between learning about individual ties and learning a one-hop exposure distribution?

A one-hop exposure describes treatment in an individual’s direct-tie neighborhood. Information about whether a given pair is tied is one ingredient. Depending on how exposure is defined, its distribution can also depend on which ties coexist around the same individual. Knowing tie frequencies dyad by dyad need not reveal that joint neighborhood structure. That is why the exposure definition and the information supplied by the audit design matter.
Could you give a purely conceptual illustration without assuming a specific design for our study?

Imagine an exposure category defined by whether someone has at least one treated direct neighbor. Its frequency depends on the occurrence of treated ties around each person, including how those ties overlap. Two possible underlying network patterns could agree on separate dyad-level tie frequencies yet differ in how often individuals have any such neighbor. This is only an illustration of why marginal tie information may be insufficient; it is not a claim about the proposed audits or a particular dataset.
Does randomized assignment resolve that joint-neighborhood issue?

Randomized assignment helps characterize treatment allocation, but it does not automatically reveal the underlying joint pattern of direct ties. If the exposure distribution depends on both assigned treatments and network structure, knowing the treatment assignment mechanism alone may leave uncertainty about exposures when ties are incompletely observed.
Is the question then whether the audits identify true ties, reporting behavior, or both?

Those are both relevant, and they should not be collapsed. Verified information about true ties could help characterize the network; information linking verification to what was reported could help characterize treatment- and tie-status-dependent reporting. The further question is whether that information is sufficient for the one-hop exposure distribution needed for policy g-computation. Positive auditing by itself answers none of those sufficiency questions conclusively.
What if auditing is itself more likely for reported ties than unreported dyads?

Then audit selection would also have to be accounted for. Audited dyads could otherwise overrepresent reported ties, and reported ties could themselves be selected according to treatment and true tie status. Positivity would rule out a zero audit chance in the relevant groups, but it would not, without further restrictions or information, remove that selection. I’m describing a conditional complication, not asserting that this is how the proposed audits operate.
Could the answer be yes under suitable additional conditions, rather than a flat no?

Yes. For example, if audits genuinely disclose the relevant true tie information, reach the dyads needed for the exposure definition, and have an adequately understood selection process with the needed overlap, they could support identification of one-hop exposure distributions despite selective reporting. But those are conditions to establish, not properties guaranteed by the word “positive.” Nor should a possible route to exposure identification be mistaken for an already established result.
And could the answer be no despite positive treatment-stratified audit probabilities?

Yes, if the audited information cannot distinguish underlying network patterns that yield different one-hop exposure distributions, positive audit probabilities alone would not identify those distributions. The issue is whether all compatible underlying possibilities agree on the exposure distribution, not simply whether some audits can occur in each treatment stratum.
How does this relate to the proposed MNAR bounds?

If treatment- and tie-status-dependent reporting leaves relevant network information unresolved, MNAR bounds are a proposed way to express what the stated restrictions still allow, rather than silently treating the reported network as complete. Whether a particular set of bounds is informative, and whether audits narrow it enough to identify an exposure distribution, cannot be concluded from positivity alone.
If exposure distributions were identifiable, would that immediately identify the population treatment-policy effect?

Not automatically. The one-hop exposure distribution is a component of the proposed policy analysis. Identifying a population treatment-policy effect also requires the other relationships used by policy g-computation to be identified under the applicable assumptions. Conversely, uncertainty about exposure distributions can be a barrier even before reaching that broader effect-identification question.
Where do the cluster-bootstrap intervals come into this specific question?

They concern uncertainty for an estimator in an identifiable regime; they do not supply identification if the exposure distribution remains ambiguous. The question here is first whether positive dyad audits, in the presence of treatment- and true-tie-status-dependent reporting, determine the relevant one-hop exposures under explicit conditions. Only after the necessary identification and estimation conditions are established would interval performance be assessed against the stated 95% interval targets.
I don’t want to presume the audits succeed merely because they have positive probabilities.

Then the precise question is whether positive treatment-stratified dyad audits provide enough verified and appropriately interpretable network information to identify one-hop exposure distributions when reporting depends on treatment and unobserved true tie status. Positivity is part of that inquiry, not its answer; the conclusion may depend on audit measurement, selection, and the joint tie information required by the exposure definition.
Here is a hypothesis for the audit question: independent, positive-probability dyad verification enables audit-weighted complete-ego g-computation despite tie-status-dependent reporting.

That is a plausible route to investigate, but it remains a hypothesis. The idea is to use verified dyads to recover complete direct-tie neighborhoods for some individuals, then weight those complete egos to account for their chances of being fully verified. Policy g-computation could use that information to evaluate one-hop exposures under a treatment policy. The crucial distinction is that verification, rather than ordinary tie reporting, would supply the tie statuses on which those calculations rely.
What does “complete ego” mean in this setting?

It means an individual’s relevant one-hop neighborhood is sufficiently verified to determine that individual’s direct-tie exposure. It does not mean the entire population network is known. The required completeness depends on which dyads could contribute to that individual’s one-hop exposure; it cannot be inferred merely because some reported ties have been verified.
Why insist on verifying dyads rather than just weighting reported ties?

Because reporting may depend on the true tie status as well as treatment. A collection of reported ties can therefore be a selective view of the underlying neighborhood. Verification can, in principle, provide information about whether candidate dyads are genuinely tied even when ordinary reporting is unreliable. Weighting reported ties alone would not automatically repair selection based on an unobserved true tie status.
Is the independence condition meant to make complete verified egos possible?

That is one role it could play. If the dyads needed for an ego’s exposure can each be verified with positive probability and their verification is independent in the relevant sense, joint verification of all those dyads can have positive probability for a finite eligible set. That supplies a conceptual basis for observing some complete egos and weighting them by their verification chances. The exact independence condition and eligible dyad set would still need to be specified before calling this an identification argument.
Can a positive probability for every dyad fail to translate into useful information about a whole ego?

Yes. Individual positive verification chances do not, by themselves, say how often the full collection needed for an ego is verified, or whether that collection has been defined appropriately. Even when complete verification has positive probability, it could be uncommon enough to make estimation imprecise. Positivity supports a possible identification route; it does not guarantee the interval-width target.
Should the weighting be thought of as correcting reporting probabilities or verification probabilities?

In this hypothesis, the audit weights primarily account for the probability that the needed dyads are verified so an ego’s relevant neighborhood can be treated as complete. Tie-status-dependent reporting remains important because it explains why the ordinarily reported network cannot simply stand in for verified neighborhoods. An implementation would need to establish the appropriate verification inclusion probabilities; the hypothesis does not specify a formula for them.
So the approach does not need us to pretend that reporting is independent of the true tie status?

Correct. Its appeal is precisely that it might permit g-computation despite tie-status-dependent reporting. Rather than assuming the reporting process is harmless, the proposed calculation would rely on verified complete-ego information and account for how that information enters through auditing. Whether verification actually supplies sufficient information is still to be established.
Would an audit limited to already reported ties deliver a complete ego?

Not necessarily. If an unreported dyad can be a true tie, verifying only reported dyads could leave the ego’s neighborhood incomplete. For the hypothesis to work as intended, verification must be capable of resolving the dyads relevant to the one-hop exposure, including those whose status ordinary reporting does not reveal. That is a condition to examine, not a feature already established for the audits.
How does this hypothesis answer the question about identifying one-hop exposure distributions?

It proposes a way to learn the joint direct-tie information needed for those distributions: fully verified egos reveal which relevant ties coexist around an individual, while audit weights connect those egos to the population of interest. If that connection is justified, it could overcome the limitation of knowing only marginal dyad tie frequencies. This is an explanation of the proposed mechanism, not a declaration that the exposure distributions have been identified.
Why does using complete egos help with the joint-neighborhood concern?

A complete relevant ego provides the collection of direct ties around the same individual, not just an isolated answer about one dyad. That collection can determine a one-hop exposure under the applicable treatment assignment. Weighted information across complete egos could therefore speak to an exposure distribution that separate dyad summaries might not determine.
Does independent verification mean I can ignore how verification was selected?

No. Independence has to have a precise meaning, and the chances of obtaining complete verified egos must be understood well enough for the proposed weights to be justified. Calling dyad verification independent and positive-probability does not, without further specification, establish that the weighted egos represent the population appropriately.
Could randomized treatment assignment make those audit weights unnecessary?

Not by itself. Randomized assignment concerns treatment allocation, whereas audit weights concern which neighborhoods become sufficiently verified. Both can be relevant to policy g-computation, but randomizing treatment does not automatically make a selectively verified set of egos representative of the underlying network.
Does one-hop interference make complete-ego verification sufficient for everything?

It makes direct neighborhoods the relevant reach of interference in the proposal, which is why complete-ego verification is attractive. But verifying those neighborhoods would address network exposure information, not automatically every condition needed to identify a population treatment-policy effect. The policy g-computation argument still has to connect exposures and outcomes under its applicable assumptions.
I want to preserve the difference between enabling an analysis and proving the analysis succeeds.

That is the right reading of the hypothesis. “Enables” expresses a proposed identification mechanism: independent, positive-probability dyad verification might make audit-weighted complete-ego g-computation feasible even though reporting depends on true tie status. It does not report a completed proof, an empirical finding, or demonstrated interval performance.
Would the tie-status-dependent reporting have to be modeled explicitly for this particular route?

Not necessarily as the sole basis for recovering every unreported tie. The proposed route instead emphasizes verified dyads and weighting complete verified egos. But one could not simply disregard reporting if it affects which dyads are eligible for verification or how verification probabilities are determined. Whether a separate reporting model is required depends on how the verification process is actually defined, which is not specified here.
If the hypothesis holds, where do the MNAR bounds fit?

The complete-ego route aims at learning enough about one-hop exposures to support policy g-computation despite selective reporting. MNAR bounds remain a distinct way to express uncertainty where the available verification and assumptions do not pin down what is needed. The hypothesis does not itself decide which regimes are point-identifiable or what bounds apply elsewhere.
What should we avoid claiming about the cluster-bootstrap intervals at this point?

We should avoid claiming that this hypothesis establishes valid cluster-bootstrap intervals or meets the numerical targets. Even if audit-weighted complete-ego g-computation identifies and estimates the effect in a regime, interval coverage and width remain separate questions. The stated goal is at least 93% coverage for 95% intervals and median width no more than 2× the complete-network oracle’s in identifiable regimes; nothing in the hypothesis demonstrates those outcomes.
So the proposed resolution to tie-status-dependent reporting is verified complete neighborhoods, appropriately weighted, rather than treating reported neighborhoods as complete?

Yes—that captures the hypothesis without overstating it. Independent, positive-probability dyad verification is proposed as a route to complete-ego information; audit weighting would relate that information to one-hop exposure distributions for policy g-computation. Whether the verification design and weights actually support identification despite tie-status-dependent reporting remains the question to establish.

I’d like to evaluate the complete-ego hypothesis by simulating 1,000 datasets, each with 300 eight-person clusters, 90% independent dyad audits, and treatment-by-tie reporting. We should assess coverage and oracle-width ratios.

That simulation would examine how the proposed audit-weighted complete-ego approach performs under the specified audit and reporting setting. The activity is to generate 1,000 datasets of 300 eight-person clusters, with dyads independently audited at 90% and reporting dependent on treatment and tie status. The outcomes to assess are interval coverage and width relative to a complete-network oracle. No simulation results are stated yet.
What is the simulation meant to tell us about the hypothesis?

It can assess whether the proposed analysis performs well in the simulated setting despite tie-status-dependent reporting. In particular, it can reveal how often the intervals cover the simulated target and how their widths compare with the complete-network oracle’s. It would not, on its own, prove identification under every process consistent with the broad hypothesis.
Why simulate complete egos rather than just count how many dyads were audited?

For a one-hop exposure, the relevant information is the collection of direct ties around an individual. Auditing many dyads overall does not ensure that every dyad needed for any particular ego’s exposure has been verified. The simulation can assess the proposed approach in terms of the complete neighborhoods it can use, rather than treating the overall audit percentage as if it were the percentage of complete egos.
Does 90% independent dyad auditing imply that 90% of egos have complete verified neighborhoods?

No. A 90% audit probability applies to each dyad, not to the event that all dyads needed for an ego are audited. Under independent audit decisions, the probability of verifying a specified collection of needed dyads depends on how many dyads are in that collection. The activity does not specify a single complete-ego rate, and we should not substitute 90% for one.
Could the audits still be informative if some egos are incomplete?

Potentially. The hypothesis proposes weighting egos whose relevant neighborhoods are fully verified, so incomplete egos do not automatically negate the route. But how often complete egos occur bears on precision, and whether the weights correctly connect them to the target population remains part of what the proposed setup must justify. The simulation can illuminate performance under its specified conditions without assuming success.
What exactly does treatment-by-tie reporting contribute to the test?

It preserves the difficult feature motivating the proposal: ordinary reporting of a dyad can depend on treatment and on whether the dyad is truly a tie. That means the reported network need not be a neutral picture of the underlying direct neighborhoods. The simulation asks whether relying on independent dyad verification and audit-weighted complete egos can perform well in that setting. No particular reporting probabilities or functional form are specified in the activity.
Should we describe the 90% as a reporting rate?

No. The 90% figure is for independent dyad audits. Treatment-by-tie reporting is a separate part of the simulated setting, and the node gives no numerical reporting rate. Conflating the two would obscure the distinction between verifying a dyad’s status and having that dyad appear through ordinary reporting.
How should we interpret ‘independent’ here without assuming more than the activity says?

At minimum, it describes the dyad audits as independently conducted with the stated 90% probability. A full identification argument would also have to be precise about how audit selection relates to treatment and true tie status, so that any audit weights have the interpretation the hypothesis requires. The simulation description does not supply every such detail, and we should not silently add it.
I want to make sure coverage is assessed against the right target.

Coverage should concern the population treatment-policy effect targeted by the analysis: across simulated datasets, does the corresponding interval contain the relevant simulated truth? That is different from asking whether an interval contains an observed-network estimate or the complete-network oracle’s estimate. The activity specifies assessment of coverage but not a particular policy contrast, so that contrast should not be invented here.
And the coverage requirement from the goal is still at least 93% for 95% intervals, correct?

Correct, within identifiable regimes. For the proposed simulation, one would assess the coverage of the 95% intervals against the ≥93% target. That threshold is a criterion for evaluation, not an observed coverage result from the 1,000 datasets.
What should ‘oracle-width ratio’ mean at this level of description?

It is a comparison of interval width with the complete-network oracle’s interval width for the same kind of population treatment-policy target. The goal’s precision criterion is median width no more than 2× the complete-network oracle’s. To assess oracle-width ratios, the comparison needs to be defined consistently; the activity does not specify a formula for aggregating ratios, so we should not claim a numerical ratio or quietly choose one as though it had been stated.
Could the coverage target be met while the oracle-width target fails?

Yes. Intervals can cover frequently but be too wide relative to the complete-network oracle. Conversely, intervals can be relatively narrow while failing the ≥93% coverage criterion for 95% intervals. That is why the activity assesses both coverage and oracle-width ratios rather than treating one measure as a substitute for the other.
Would 1,000 simulated datasets establish the identification boundary we were seeking?

Not by itself. The 1,000 datasets can provide a finite-simulation assessment under the simulated conditions. An identification boundary is a claim about what the available information and explicit assumptions determine; it needs an argument about those assumptions, not just favorable simulation performance. The simulation is an evaluation of the proposed complete-ego route, not a replacement for that argument.
Could unfavorable simulation performance disprove the conceptual usefulness of dyad verification in every regime?

No. A result in this activity would speak to the conditions and procedures actually simulated. It would not automatically extend to every possible audit probability, reporting process, or interference restriction. Equally, favorable performance would not establish success outside the setting examined. At this point, neither sort of result has been reported.
Where do cluster-bootstrap intervals fit into the assessment?

They are the interval procedure proposed for the policy analysis. If those are the intervals evaluated, the simulation can assess their coverage and width in this setting with clusters, against the stated 95% interval and complete-network-oracle benchmarks. The activity itself does not specify a bootstrap implementation or report whether its intervals meet either criterion.
Does including 300 eight-person clusters specify how the underlying ties or outcomes are generated?

No. It fixes the stated scale and clustering of each simulated dataset: 300 clusters, each containing eight people. It does not specify a tie-generating process, outcome-generating process, treatment policy, or effect size. Those details should not be supplied as if they were part of this activity.
Why keep the complete-network oracle as a benchmark if the method is designed for incomplete observation?

Because it supplies the comparison requested by the goal: how much wider are the intervals under the audit-and-reporting setting than intervals with complete-network information? The oracle is a reference for precision, not an assertion that the proposed method observes the full network. The specified target is a median width no greater than 2× that reference in identifiable regimes.
Can this simulation also tell us whether MNAR bounds are needed?

It can help evaluate the proposed complete-ego analysis under the simulated treatment-by-tie reporting, but the stated activity is specifically to assess coverage and oracle-width ratios. Whether point identification is justified, or bounds are needed for other regimes, still depends on the identification restrictions and what verification reveals. The simulation description does not report a conclusion about MNAR bounds.
So how would you state the activity without making it sound like a completed experiment?

Simulate 1,000 datasets, each comprising 300 eight-person clusters, with 90% independent dyad audits and treatment-by-tie reporting; use them to assess interval coverage and oracle-width ratios for the proposed audit-weighted complete-ego policy analysis. Evaluate 95% intervals against the goal of at least 93% coverage and median width no more than 2× the complete-network oracle’s in identifiable regimes, without presuming those targets have been achieved.
The simulation results are in: across 1,000 simulated datasets, the audit-weighted estimates achieved 94.1% coverage, and median interval width was 1.6× the complete-network oracle’s.

Those are the two reported results: 94.1% coverage across the 1,000 simulated datasets and a median interval width 1.6× the complete-network oracle’s. They describe interval performance in this simulation setting. They do not, by themselves, establish identification in every setting with treatment-dependent tie reporting.
What does the 94.1% figure measure?

Why emphasize the difference between a table of ratios and a median-width requirement?

Because a ratio reported for each setting needs a defined numerator, denominator, and summary. A table entry called an oracle-width ratio does not, without its definition, tell us whether it represents the ratio of median widths, a median of interval-by-interval ratios, or something else. Is 2× a ceiling for every interval in the tables?

For coverage, do we compare the 70% verification setting to 70% coverage?

No. The 70%, 80%, and 90% numbers label verification settings. The coverage target is ≥93% for 95% intervals at each setting being assessed. A verification percentage is neither a coverage result nor the nominal confidence level.

Conditionally, that setting would meet the coverage criterion but not the width criterion, assuming the entries use the required definitions and the setting is identifiable. Do we need to decide whether the setting at each verification rate is identifiable before interpreting those targets?

Yes, the original performance targets apply within identifiable regimes. Yes. Can we assign each coverage and width number to a particular rate from that wording alone?

Does this evidence give a result for 70% verification?

No 70% coverage or oracle-width value is stated in this finding. AuditBound-v1 has a table covering that verification rate, but the reported conclusion here supplies numerical performance only for the 80–90% audit settings. We cannot infer the 70% entry from the stated ranges.
How should I interpret the complete-network oracle in the width comparison?

It is the interval-width benchmark. A reported width of 1.8–1.6× the oracle’s compares the audited analysis with one using complete-network information; it does not imply that the audited analysis observed the complete network. No absolute interval widths are supplied.
Do the reported coverage percentages mean the intervals were labeled 93.4% to 94.1% intervals?
No. Those numbers are observed coverage results. The broader evaluation concerns 95% intervals; their nominal label should not be replaced with the coverage observed across evaluated datasets.
Does the identification finding tell us that the point estimates have no error?

No. Identification says the target can be determined from the relevant observable information under the stated restrictions. Estimation from finite data can still have uncertainty, which is why coverage and interval width are assessed separately. The finding does not report zero estimation error.
Could I describe the reported width as an increase of 1.8–1.6 percentage points?

No. The width result is multiplicative: 1.8–1.6 times the complete-network oracle’s width. Percentage points would be the wrong unit, and the finding does not provide absolute widths from which to calculate a difference.
Does the evidence validate every component of the original proposal, including a particular cluster-bootstrap implementation and MNAR bounds?

It supports the distinction the proposal sought to address: an audited identification route and an unaudited MNAR identification boundary, alongside audited interval-performance figures. What is the careful way to convey the scope of the unaudited result alongside the audited numbers?

State them separately: AuditBound-v1 confirms audited identification and nonidentification for its unaudited MNAR models. For the 80–90% audit settings, it reports 93.4–94.1% coverage and interval width 1.8–1.6× the complete-network oracle’s. I want to stress-test audit-weighted g-computation across 1,000 datasets with unrecorded degree-dependent audits and two-hop spillovers. Let’s measure coverage and oracle-width ratios.

That would test the procedure when two features complicate its usual interpretation: audit selection depends on network degree in a way that is not recorded, and interference extends to two hops. Across the 1,000 datasets, coverage would assess how often the intervals contain the target, while oracle-width ratios would compare their widths with those of a complete-network oracle. The activity specifies what to examine, not how the procedure performs.
Why are unrecorded degree-dependent audits a meaningful stress test?

Audit weighting needs an adequate account of which network information becomes verified. If auditing depends on degree but that dependence is unrecorded, the verified neighborhoods may be selected in a way the weights cannot properly account for. The stress test can reveal how the analysis behaves under that complication; it should not assume in advance that the weights correct it.
Does degree dependence mean high-degree individuals are necessarily audited more often?

No direction is specified. “Degree-dependent” says auditing varies with degree, but it does not say whether audit chances rise or fall with degree, or give their probabilities. We should not add a direction or a numerical audit mechanism to the activity.
What is unrecorded here?

The stress-test description identifies degree-dependent auditing as unrecorded. For interpreting the analysis, the important point is that the degree-related selection cannot simply be treated as known information available to construct correct audit weights. It does not provide a fuller observation protocol, so we should not claim exactly which variables or audit decisions are recorded.
Could audits still happen with positive probability while this causes trouble?

Yes. Having an opportunity for verification and knowing how verified cases represent the target population are distinct issues. Positive audit chances alone would not supply the missing account of degree-dependent selection. Whether, and how much, that affects the resulting estimates and intervals is what the stress test would assess.
Why include two-hop spillovers as well?

Two-hop spillovers allow treatment effects to extend through paths of two social connections, rather than being confined to direct neighbors. That tests what happens when an analysis built around one-hop exposures encounters interference beyond that reach. The activity does not specify the form or strength of the two-hop effects.
Does a complete verified ego necessarily capture a two-hop exposure?

Not necessarily. Knowing an individual’s direct ties can establish a one-hop neighborhood, but a two-hop exposure can require information about connections beyond those direct ties. Whether the available verified information is sufficient depends on the exposure being evaluated. We should not presume that complete one-hop verification resolves two-hop spillovers.
Are these two complications meant to be tested together or as separate scenarios?

The activity says to stress-test across 1,000 datasets with unrecorded degree-dependent audits and two-hop spillovers. It does not specify a factorial design or separate scenarios isolating each complication. We can discuss the distinct reasons each matters, but we should not claim the activity will separately attribute any performance change to one or the other.
What exactly should coverage refer to in this stress test?

Coverage is the fraction of the 1,000 simulated datasets in which the interval for the relevant population treatment-policy effect contains its target. To interpret it, the simulated target and the interval’s target have to align even when two-hop spillovers are present. The activity does not give a numerical coverage result or specify a particular policy contrast.
Could an interval cover an analysis-defined one-hop quantity but not the effect under the two-hop process?

Conceptually, yes. Those would be different targets if the two-hop spillovers matter for the population treatment-policy effect. The stress test should be clear about what its coverage measure checks; otherwise an apparently favorable coverage figure could answer a narrower question than the intended policy-effect question. This is a measurement caution, not a claim that such a mismatch occurred.
What do the oracle-width ratios add beyond coverage?

They measure relative interval width using the complete-network oracle as a benchmark. Coverage and width are separate: an interval can be wide yet miss its target, or narrow without covering it sufficiently often. Measuring both helps characterize the stress-test behavior without treating precision as proof of valid inference.
Does the complete-network oracle automatically solve the unrecorded audit-selection issue?

The oracle supplies a complete-network reference for the width comparison; it does not make unrecorded audit selection disappear from the audit-weighted analysis. The activity does not specify the oracle’s full procedure. We should use it as the named benchmark and avoid assuming additional oracle properties that have not been stated.
Could a favorable width ratio establish that audit weighting still identifies the policy effect with two-hop spillovers?

No. A width ratio describes interval precision relative to the oracle. It cannot by itself establish identification or show that a one-hop-based policy calculation correctly handles two-hop interference. Coverage is also a performance measure, not a substitute for an identification argument under the stress-test conditions.
Can we predict that the coverage will fall below a particular percentage?

Not from the activity description. It gives 1,000 datasets and the two stressors, but no results or detailed generating mechanisms from which to assert a coverage value. The point is to measure coverage rather than presume its direction or magnitude.
Are the 1,000 datasets specified to have any particular cluster size or verification rate?

No. This activity specifies 1,000 datasets, unrecorded degree-dependent audits, two-hop spillovers, and the two performance measures. It does not state a cluster count, cluster size, or numerical audit rate for this stress test, so none should be supplied as a feature of it.
Should we describe these conditions as part of the assumptions that justify audit-weighted g-computation?

No. They are stress-test conditions. Unrecorded degree-dependent audit selection challenges the interpretation of audit weights, and two-hop spillovers challenge a one-hop interference restriction. The activity examines performance under those conditions; it does not assert that the conditions satisfy an identification argument for the procedure.
If the measured coverage and width differed, could this design tell us which stressor was responsible?

Not necessarily. Because the activity does not specify separate runs varying only one feature at a time, a combined stress test cannot automatically isolate the contribution of degree-dependent auditing from that of two-hop spillovers. It can measure how audit-weighted g-computation behaves in the stated setting without assigning a cause to either feature on its own.
How should we phrase this activity without implying that we have results?

Stress-test audit-weighted g-computation across 1,000 simulated datasets featuring unrecorded degree-dependent audits and two-hop spillovers, and measure interval coverage and width ratios relative to a complete-network oracle. The description identifies the conditions and outcomes to examine, without asserting any coverage percentage, width ratio, or identification conclusion under those conditions.

In the one-hop interference setting with 80% treatment-stratified audit positivity, unrecorded degree-dependent verification reduced coverage to 87.2%. The reported interval width was 1.8× the complete-network oracle’s.

That result separates coverage from width. Coverage of 87.2% is below the goal of at least 93% for 95% intervals, even though the reported width ratio of 1.8× is below the numerical 2× benchmark. The finding is specifically for one-hop interference with 80% treatment-stratified audit positivity and unrecorded degree-dependent verification.
Does the 80% figure describe coverage?

No. It describes treatment-stratified audit positivity in this setting. The observed coverage is 87.2%. Nor does 80% tell us what proportion of individuals had complete verified one-hop neighborhoods.
Why didn’t treatment-stratified audit positivity protect coverage here?

Treatment stratification addresses auditing across treatment strata, but it does not by itself account for verification that also depends on degree. When that degree dependence is unrecorded, audit weights may not adequately represent how verified network information was selected. The reported 87.2% coverage shows the performance shortfall in this setting; the finding does not provide a detailed breakdown of the weighting error.
Is this a result about two-hop spillovers?

No. This reported result explicitly specifies one-hop interference. Its 87.2% coverage should be attributed to the stated setting with unrecorded degree-dependent verification, not presented as a measured effect of two-hop spillovers.
Does one-hop interference still leave degree-dependent verification as a problem?

Yes. One-hop interference limits which social connections can affect an individual’s exposure; it does not determine which dyads get verified or make verification representative. The result shows a coverage shortfall under the one-hop restriction when verification depends on degree in an unrecorded way.
Can I say the width criterion was met?

You can say the reported oracle-width ratio was 1.8×, numerically below 2×. The goal, however, is specifically about median interval width relative to the complete-network oracle. This finding does not explicitly identify the summary behind the 1.8× figure, so confirming that precise median-width criterion would require that definition. In any event, the 87.2% coverage misses the coverage criterion.
Would a relatively narrow interval make the low coverage less concerning?

No. Width and coverage are joint performance requirements, not alternatives. An interval can be comparatively narrow and still miss the target too often. Here the reported 1.8× width does not compensate for coverage below 93%.
How far below the coverage target is 87.2%?
It is 5.8 percentage points below the ≥93% threshold. That is a comparison of coverage percentages, not a change in the audit rate or the oracle-width ratio.
Does this coverage result by itself prove that the population treatment-policy effect is nonidentified?

No. Coverage is a property of the evaluated intervals in this setting. Identification asks whether the observable information and stated restrictions determine the target effect. The 87.2% result shows that the interval-performance target was missed; it does not, on its own, establish a nonidentification theorem.
Does it prove the audit-weighted point estimates are biased?

Not from the quantities reported here. Low coverage is consistent with a problem in the overall estimation-and-interval procedure, but this finding gives neither a point-estimate bias measure nor a decomposition of the coverage shortfall. The supported numerical conclusions are 87.2% coverage and 1.8× oracle width under the stated conditions.
What does ‘unrecorded’ add to the interpretation of degree-dependent verification?

It means the degree dependence relevant to verification is not available as recorded information for the analysis to account for directly. That is more specific than merely saying that audit probabilities vary. The finding does not say precisely how verification probabilities vary with degree or which degrees are verified more often.
Can we infer that high-degree egos were overrepresented among verified cases?

No. Degree-dependent verification gives no direction on its own. It could not justify a claim that higher-degree egos were more or less likely to be verified without further details. The reported coverage shortfall does not reveal that direction.
Does 80% treatment-stratified audit positivity imply independent verification?

No. Positivity and independence are distinct properties. The result expressly involves degree-dependent verification, so the 80% figure should not be used to assume that dyads were verified independently of degree or that complete verified egos had known inclusion probabilities.
What implication does this have for the proposed audit-weighted analysis?

It shows a limitation of relying on treatment-stratified audit positivity alone as a performance safeguard. Under the stated unrecorded degree-dependent verification, the audit-weighted intervals attained only 87.2% coverage, below the ≥93% target, despite a reported width of 1.8× the complete-network oracle’s. That is a conclusion about this setting, not a claim that the approach fails under every audit process.
Should I describe the complete-network oracle as eliminating the coverage problem?

No. The oracle is the named benchmark for interval width in the reported 1.8× comparison. This finding does not report the oracle’s coverage or say what an oracle analysis would do about the observed coverage shortfall.
Could we use the 87.2% result to assign separate effects to audit selection and interference?

Not separate numerical effects. The finding fixes interference at one hop and reports reduced coverage with unrecorded degree-dependent verification. It does not provide a decomposition across multiple mechanisms or a rate-by-rate comparison from which to calculate separate contributions.
What is the most precise statement of the evidence?

With one-hop interference and 80% treatment-stratified audit positivity, unrecorded degree-dependent verification reduced coverage to 87.2%, with reported interval width 1.8× the complete-network oracle’s. Coverage therefore falls below the ≥93% target for 95% intervals; the width ratio is numerically below 2×, but it does not remedy the coverage shortfall.
Let’s retain one-hop audit-weighted inference with independent dyad verification, but exclude unrecorded degree-dependent audits after coverage fell to 87.2%.

That draws a specific boundary around the retained approach. One-hop audit-weighted inference remains in scope when dyad verification is independent. Unrecorded degree-dependent audits are excluded, with the observed drop to 87.2% coverage providing the stated reason. The decision does not say that audit weighting works regardless of how verification is selected.
What does “retain” mean here? Are we retaining every possible use of audit weighting?

No. The retained approach is one-hop audit-weighted inference with independent dyad verification. Audit weighting is not being endorsed as a generic correction for any audit-selection process. The independence condition is part of the decision’s scope.
Why name independent dyad verification explicitly?

It distinguishes the verification process under which the inference is being retained from the unrecorded degree-dependent audits being excluded. If the analysis relies on verified dyads to represent relevant one-hop neighborhoods, how those dyads come to be verified matters. The decision should therefore keep the verification condition visible rather than referring only to “audits.”
Is one-hop interference also essential to the wording?

Yes. The decision retains *one-hop* audit-weighted inference. It should not be paraphrased as retaining the same inference under interference of any reach. The one-hop qualification states the scope of what is kept; this decision makes no separate determination about other interference settings.
When you say “exclude unrecorded degree-dependent audits,” are you saying no dyads can be audited in those settings?

No. The exclusion concerns using that audit-selection setting for the retained inference. Dyads might still be verified, but verification that depends on degree in an unrecorded way is outside this decision’s accepted conditions. The problem is not the mere absence of audits; it is the unrecorded dependence in how verification occurs.
Does the decision specify whether verification is more likely at higher or lower degree?

No. It identifies unrecorded degree dependence but gives no direction or functional form for that dependence. We should not infer which individuals or dyads were more likely to be verified from the decision or from the 87.2% coverage figure.
Could I simply say that having some verified dyads is sufficient for the retained method?

That would remove a stated condition. The decision specifies independent dyad verification, not merely the presence of verified dyads. It also retains the analysis in a one-hop setting. A description that says only “some dyads were audited” would be broader than what was decided.
What role does the 87.2% figure play?

It is the coverage result motivating the exclusion of unrecorded degree-dependent audits. It should be identified as coverage, not as a verification rate, an interval width, or an effect estimate. The decision uses it to explain why that audit setting is outside the retained approach.
Does 87.2% describe the performance of independent dyad verification?

No. In the decision, 87.2% is associated with the unrecorded degree-dependent audit setting being excluded. Attaching that number to independent dyad verification would reverse the distinction the decision is making.
Should we say that degree-dependent auditing is impossible to analyze?

No. Excluding *unrecorded* degree-dependent audits from the retained inference is not a claim that every degree-dependent audit process is impossible to analyze. This decision does not evaluate an approach with degree dependence that is recorded or otherwise adequately accounted for. Its exclusion is confined to the condition named here.
Does the decision establish a new identification result for the excluded setting?

No. The stated reason for exclusion is the coverage drop to 87.2%, which is an interval-performance finding. The decision does not say that the population treatment-policy effect is nonidentified under unrecorded degree-dependent audits, nor does it provide a separate identification argument for that setting.
So we shouldn’t turn a coverage finding into a proof about identifiability?

Correct. Coverage describes how the evaluated intervals performed. Identifiability asks what the observable information and assumptions determine about the target effect. Here the coverage result supports a scope decision: retain the one-hop, independently verified audit-weighted approach and exclude the unrecorded degree-dependent audit setting. It does not, by itself, answer every identification question about the excluded setting.
Does “retain” imply that every interval from the retained approach will cover?

No. Retaining an inferential approach is not a guarantee for each individual interval. The decision identifies the conditions under which to keep using the approach; it does not assert perfect coverage or give a new universal performance figure for independent dyad verification.
Could we preserve the audit-weighted method but drop the independent-verification condition if we make the intervals wider?

That is not a change made by this decision. It expressly retains independent dyad verification and excludes unrecorded degree-dependent audits after the coverage decline. Wider intervals are not stated as a remedy, so we should not present them as an adopted alternative.
Is there any reason to mention unaudited MNAR settings when stating this decision?

It is not necessary to state this decision accurately. The distinction here is between independent dyad verification, which remains within the one-hop audit-weighted approach, and unrecorded degree-dependent audits, which are excluded. The decision does not make an additional ruling about unaudited MNAR settings.
Would calling the excluded setting “dependent audits” alone be precise enough?

It would lose two important qualifications: the dependence is on degree, and it is unrecorded. The decision does not exclude every possible form of dependence in every setting. “Unrecorded degree-dependent audits” preserves the particular condition being excluded.
Can you phrase the decision concisely without making broader claims?
Retain one-hop audit-weighted inference with independent dyad verification; exclude unrecorded degree-dependent audits, given that coverage fell to 87.2% under that audit condition.
I’d like to consider another proposal: randomly census 80% of isolated clusters, then use design-weighted g-computation under assignment positivity to allow arbitrary within-cluster interference.

This proposes shifting the unit of complete observation to the cluster. Randomly selecting 80% of isolated clusters for a census could provide the relevant within-cluster information for those clusters; design weighting would account for which clusters were selected. Assignment positivity would support evaluating the treatment assignments relevant to a population policy. If clusters truly are isolated for interference, the approach could allow treatment effects to propagate arbitrarily *within* a cluster without assuming a one-hop limit. These are proposed conditions and a proposed analysis, not an established identification or performance result.
What does “isolated clusters” need to mean for that claim?

It needs to mean that treatment in one cluster does not affect outcomes in another cluster for the policy effect being studied. It does not mean individuals within a cluster lack social ties. The proposed relaxation concerns interference within each cluster; isolation keeps interference from crossing cluster boundaries.
When you say arbitrary within-cluster interference, do you mean only direct neighbors matter?

No. Arbitrary within-cluster interference permits outcomes to depend on the treatment assignments of others throughout the same cluster, without restricting the influence to direct neighbors or a particular number of network hops. The word “arbitrary” is bounded by the cluster: it does not authorize effects from treatment assignments in other clusters.
Does this proposal require a particular exposure mapping based on the network?

It does not specify one. Allowing arbitrary within-cluster interference means we should not silently impose a one-hop exposure mapping. A concrete g-computation calculation would still need to define the population treatment-policy effect and the relevant within-cluster treatment assignments, but no particular mapping or policy contrast is given in this proposal.
What, precisely, is the 80% a percentage of?

It is the fraction of isolated clusters proposed for random census. It is not a dyad-audit probability, a treatment-assignment probability, a proportion of individuals treated, or an interval-coverage percentage. Those quantities have different roles.
Why select clusters at random instead of just taking whichever clusters have good network records?

Random cluster selection supplies a design-based basis for relating censused clusters to the population of isolated clusters. Selecting only clusters with good records could leave that relationship unclear if record quality is related to features relevant to the policy effect. That explains the role of random selection; it does not establish that a particular weighting calculation has already succeeded.
What does a cluster census have to observe to address treatment-dependent missing ties?

For the proposal to address that issue through a census, the census must make the within-cluster information required by the policy calculation available rather than merely repeat the treatment-dependent pattern of reported ties. Calling something a census is not sufficient if relevant true ties remain unobserved. The proposal does not spell out a measurement protocol, so its identification claim should be conditional on what the census actually resolves.
Do we need every cluster in the population to have its ties fully observed?

The proposal calls for a census of a randomly selected 80% of isolated clusters, not a census of every cluster. Design weighting is intended to connect information from the selected clusters to the population target. That requires an appropriate sampling design and relevant measurements in censused clusters; it should not be paraphrased as though the uncensused 20% were also observed in full.
Does random sampling of clusters alone identify a population treatment-policy effect?

Not alone. Random cluster selection helps with the population-representation part of the question. Evaluating a treatment policy also depends on what treatment assignments can occur, what outcomes and within-cluster information are measured, and how the policy g-computation is justified. The proposal explicitly includes assignment positivity for that reason; it does not claim that the 80% census fraction by itself settles identification.
Can you explain assignment positivity in this setting without assuming a particular assignment mechanism?

Conceptually, the treatment-assignment patterns needed to evaluate the policy must have support under the assignment process used to learn about outcomes. With arbitrary within-cluster interference, support may need to be considered for relevant *within-cluster configurations*, rather than only whether an individual can receive each treatment. The proposal does not specify the policy or assignment probabilities, so the exact positivity condition remains to be stated.
So could everyone have a positive individual chance of treatment while a policy-relevant cluster assignment still lacks support?

In principle, yes. Individual-level positivity does not necessarily imply that every joint treatment configuration needed for an arbitrary within-cluster interference analysis can occur. Whether a particular configuration matters depends on the policy being evaluated. This is why the proposal’s assignment-positivity requirement should be interpreted against the policy and the within-cluster assignments it requires, without inventing a particular design here.
What is design weighting correcting for?

In this proposal, its primary role is to account for the random selection of clusters into the 80% census so that the censused information can be related to the population of isolated clusters. It does not automatically repair incomplete measurement *within* censused clusters, nor does it create treatment-assignment support where assignment positivity fails. The exact weights would follow from the sampling design, which is not detailed here.
Does using design-weighted g-computation mean we ignore uncertainty from which clusters were selected?

No. The selection of clusters is part of the design to be reflected in the analysis. G-computation concerns evaluating outcomes under a policy and aggregating them to the population target; design weighting concerns how the selected clusters represent that population. An uncertainty procedure would need to account for the relevant sources of variation, but no particular interval method is specified by this proposal.
Would a within-cluster census automatically make the complete-network oracle comparison irrelevant?

No. The population analysis would still rely on only 80% of clusters being censused, while a complete-network oracle remains the named reference for interval width in the broader goal. A census of sampled clusters is not the same as observing the complete population network. Is it fair to frame this as an unconditional approval of census inference whenever there are bridges?

No. The word ‘only’ is central: ≥20 bridge-positive censused clusters and stratified-bootstrap intervals are required for this rare-bridge extension. Removing either requirement would broaden the decision beyond what it says.
Does the complete-network oracle become part of the data available to the census analysis?

No. The complete-network oracle is the reference for the reported 1.9× interval-width comparison. The census analysis and the oracle should not be conflated; comparison with an oracle does not grant the census analysis complete-network information.
Do the performance figures themselves explain why stratification works?

They report coverage and relative width for the evaluated approach; they do not, on their own, explain the mechanism or establish that stratification will perform the same way under every rare-bridge process. The decision is to use the approach within its stated conditions, not to assert a universal explanation from two numbers.
Give me a concise statement of the decision that keeps both conditions and both figures.

Extend census inference to rare-bridge regimes only with ≥20 bridge-positive censused clusters and stratified-bootstrap intervals, supported by reported 93.6% coverage and interval width 1.9× the complete-network oracle’s.

I’d like to consider another route: recover one-hop exposure distributions from three conditionally independent, treatment-stratified tie reporters with zero false positives, then bootstrap policy g-computation.

That is a proposal for handling incompletely observed ties, not an identification result yet. Three reporters provide multiple views of each relevant tie; treatment stratification allows reporting behavior to differ across treatment strata. Conditional independence and zero false positives are the restrictions intended to make those reports informative about underlying ties. The recovered one-hop exposure distributions would then feed into policy g-computation, with a bootstrap proposed for interval construction.
What does zero false positives tell us about a reported tie?

Under that restriction, a reporter does not call a dyad tied when it is not truly tied. A positive tie report therefore indicates a true tie within the proposed model. The restriction does not say that every true tie gets reported: false negatives can remain, including dyads missed by all three reporters.
If a dyad is missed by all three, can we simply label it a non-tie?

No. Three negative reports may correspond either to a true non-tie or to a true tie that none of the reporters detected. The proposal seeks to use patterns across the three reporters, together with its assumptions, to learn about that ambiguity. Whether those patterns identify the information needed for one-hop exposures still has to be established.
What does treatment-stratified reporting contribute?

It keeps reporting behavior associated with treatment from being collapsed into a single undifferentiated process. The proposed recovery would assess reporter patterns within the relevant treatment strata rather than assume reporting is the same regardless of treatment. The proposal does not specify how the strata are defined or provide stratum-specific reporting probabilities.
Does treatment stratification mean treatment has no further effect on what gets reported?

Not automatically. Stratification is a way to account for treatment-related differences in reporting within a specified framework; it is not, by itself, proof that every treatment-related observation effect has been captured. The proposed identification argument would need to state which treatment information defines the strata and what reporting restrictions hold within them.
What exactly are the three reporters?

The proposal does not identify them as particular people, records, or measurement systems. It specifies three sources of tie reports and conditions on their reporting behavior. Assigning them identities or distinct accuracy levels would add details that have not been given.
Why require conditional independence rather than just having three reports?

Multiple reports provide extra information only in light of assumptions about how their errors relate. If reporters tend to miss the same true ties for an unaccounted-for reason, agreement among them may be misleading. Conditional independence is the proposed restriction intended to make the joint report patterns informative about underlying tie status; merely counting three reports would not impose it.
Independent conditional on what?

That must be made explicit in a formal version of the proposal. The relevant conditioning would need to distinguish underlying tie status and the treatment strata used to characterize reporting, while stating any other variables required by the model. As written, the proposal says ‘conditionally independent’ but does not give a full conditioning set, so we should not claim that a particular version has already been established.
Does conditional independence say the reporters have identical chances of detecting a tie?

No. Independence and identical detection probabilities are different restrictions. The proposal allows us to discuss three conditionally independent reporters but does not specify whether their reporting probabilities are equal or different. It also supplies no numerical detection rates.
Could treatment affect each reporter differently and still fit the basic proposal?

Treatment-stratified reporting leaves room to consider reporter-specific behavior by treatment stratum, provided the eventual model states how that behavior is represented and maintains its required restrictions. Nothing here establishes a particular pattern of treatment effects for the three reporters.
Is zero false positives meant to rule out false negatives as well?

No. It rules out positive reports of nonexistent ties; it does not require perfect sensitivity to true ties. False negatives are central to why recovering the underlying tie information is necessary. A model that silently assumes all true ties are reported would be stronger than this proposal.
Does learning the prevalence of true ties within a treatment stratum automatically give the one-hop exposure distribution?

Not necessarily. A one-hop exposure can depend on which true ties occur together around the same individual, as well as on treatment among those direct neighbors. A marginal frequency of true ties across dyads might not determine that joint neighborhood information.
