The proposed recovery needs to establish that the three-reporter data and stated restrictions identify the exposure distributions actually required by policy g-computation.
So the unit of inference is not necessarily an isolated dyad?

Right. The reporters supply information about dyads, but one-hop exposure is defined around an individual’s direct-tie neighborhood. A complete argument must connect the dyad-level reporting patterns to the distribution of those neighborhoods and their treatment exposures. The proposal does not specify an exposure formula or assert that dyad marginals alone suffice.
Could an all-negative reporting pattern still be informative if it does not identify the status of that particular dyad?

Potentially. Across dyads, the frequencies of the different three-reporter patterns may help distinguish how often true ties are missed from how often dyads are true non-ties, under the proposed restrictions. That is a conceptual motivation for multiple reporters. It does not mean the status of every all-negative dyad becomes known or that exposure distributions are automatically identified.
Would zero false positives on its own be enough to recover unreported ties?

No. It validates positive reports under the model but leaves all-negative dyads ambiguous. The proposed route relies on the additional information from three reporters and their conditional-independence structure, stratified by treatment. Its sufficiency still depends on a rigorous identification argument.
Does this proposal say there will be a dyad census or independent verification?

It does not specify either. Its stated information source is three conditionally independent, treatment-stratified tie reporters with zero false positives. We should assess what that information and those restrictions can identify without adding a census or a verification design to the proposal.
What if two reporters’ errors are correlated even after the proposed conditioning?

Then the conditional-independence restriction would not hold for those reporters, and the recovery argument based on it could be undermined. Having three reporters would not by itself correct that violation. This is a limitation to examine, not a statement that the reporters here are correlated.
Does calling the reports treatment-stratified guarantee that every stratum has enough information?

No. A treatment stratum can be defined without necessarily providing the report patterns needed to learn about ties in that stratum. The proposal does not give stratum sizes, probabilities, or an overlap condition. Whether the relevant reporting and treatment strata support recovery is part of the identification boundary to establish.
Suppose one reporter never detects true ties in a relevant stratum. Does having three names for reporters resolve that?

Not simply by naming three sources. If a source supplies no distinguishing information in a relevant stratum, the proposed recovery has less information there than a superficial count of three reporters suggests. The exact consequences would depend on the other reporters and the full assumptions; the proposal does not specify that scenario or its outcome.
Once we have a one-hop exposure distribution, what does policy g-computation add?

It would use the exposure information, together with the other relationships justified for the policy analysis, to evaluate outcomes under a treatment policy and aggregate them to a population treatment-policy effect. Recovering an exposure distribution addresses a network-information component. It does not alone establish every condition needed to identify the policy effect or specify a particular policy contrast.
Does ‘one-hop’ mean the method covers spillovers through two or more social connections?

No. The proposed exposure recovery is explicitly one-hop: it concerns direct ties and the treatment exposures defined through them. It should not be described as resolving interference through more distant network paths without further assumptions or information.
What role would the bootstrap play?

The bootstrap is the proposed way to construct intervals for the policy g-computation analysis, including the uncertainty associated with estimating the quantities it uses. The proposal does not specify a resampling unit, a bootstrap variant, or an interval formula. Nor can bootstrap resampling supply identification if the reporter model fails to determine the target.
Could we treat each reporter’s statement as independent when bootstrapping?

Not on the information given. Conditional independence in the proposed reporting model does not automatically determine an appropriate bootstrap resampling scheme, especially when reports concern dyads embedded in shared neighborhoods. An interval method would need to respect the dependence relevant to the estimator; no such implementation is specified here.
What are the performance criteria for intervals produced this way?

Within an identifiable regime, the broader goal is ≥93% coverage for 95% intervals and median interval width ≤2× that of a complete-network oracle. Those criteria would apply to the proposed bootstrapped policy g-computation intervals if the target is identified. The proposal gives no measured coverage or width ratio.
Does using three reporters imply that the intervals will be within 2× the oracle’s width?

No. Three reporters and zero false positives describe a possible source of information and restrictions on reporting, not a quantitative precision result. Even if the target can be identified, how often ties go undetected and how uncertainty propagates into policy g-computation can matter for interval width. The ≤2× median-width criterion must be evaluated, not inferred from the reporter count.
And would good coverage prove the reporter assumptions were true?

No. Favorable interval performance in an evaluation could support the proposed analysis under the conditions examined, but it would not prove that conditional independence or zero false positives holds universally. The assumptions and the coverage criterion address different questions.
How should we state the proposed identification boundary without claiming it is already known?

Ask whether three conditionally independent tie reporters, analyzed within treatment strata and assumed to have zero false positives, determine the true direct-tie information needed for one-hop exposure distributions. Then ask whether those distributions and the other conditions for policy g-computation identify the population treatment-policy effect. The proposal offers a route through those questions; it does not yet answer them for every reporting process.
Can you give a compact version of the proposal that preserves the assumptions, method, and uncertainty target?

Propose recovering one-hop exposure distributions from three conditionally independent, treatment-stratified tie reporters with zero false positives, then using those distributions in bootstrapped policy g-computation. Identification under the reporter restrictions and the performance of 95% intervals against ≥93% coverage and median width ≤2× the complete-network oracle’s remain to be established.
Does latent degree-driven dependence among tie reporters invalidate exposure identification despite treatment-stratified three-reporter agreement?

It can undermine an identification argument that relies on the three reporters being conditionally independent, but agreement within treatment strata is not enough to decide the question. If an unobserved feature of an individual’s degree affects several reporters’ chances of detecting that individual’s ties, their reports may remain dependent even after accounting for treatment and true tie status. Whether the one-hop exposure distribution is still identifiable would depend on what additional information or restrictions are available.
Why wouldn’t three reporters agreeing within each treatment stratum demonstrate conditional independence?

Agreement is a feature of the observed reports; conditional independence is a claim about how the reporters behave after conditioning on the variables specified by the reporting model, including underlying tie status. True status is not generally observed for dyads missed by all reporters. Reporters can agree because they independently detect the same ties, or because a shared, unobserved degree-related feature affects all three. Treatment stratification does not distinguish those explanations by itself.
Does latent degree have to change whether a dyad is a true tie, or is changing reporting enough to create the concern?

Changing reporting can be enough. If degree affects each reporter’s probability of detecting a true tie, then averaging over unobserved degree can make their reports dependent within a treatment stratum and true-tie category. Degree could also be related to which ties coexist around an individual, which would matter for one-hop exposures. Those are possible mechanisms to examine, not additional facts asserted about the reporters.
Could the reports be independent conditional on degree but dependent when degree is latent?

Yes. Independence after conditioning on true tie status, treatment, *and degree* would not necessarily imply independence after conditioning only on true tie status and treatment. Mixing over unobserved degree levels can introduce dependence in the observed reporter patterns. The exact conditioning set matters; the word “conditionally” cannot do that work without specifying it.
Does that mean any degree dependence automatically makes exposure identification impossible?

No. Degree dependence is not, on its own, a proof of nonidentification. Its implications depend on how it enters reporting, whether relevant degree information can be observed or otherwise learned, and what restrictions link report patterns to true neighborhoods. The concern is that three treatment-stratified reports may not uniquely determine the one-hop exposure distribution when unaccounted-for dependence is allowed.
What does zero false positives still tell us if the reporters share this degree-related dependence?

It still means a positive report identifies a true tie under that restriction. But a dyad with three negative reports remains ambiguous: it may be a non-tie or a true tie missed by all reporters. If latent degree makes joint misses more or less likely than conditional independence would imply, the frequency of three negatives can be hard to translate into a frequency of unobserved true ties.
Could all three reporters show strong agreement and still miss many of the same true ties?

Conceptually, yes. Shared reporting difficulty could make a set of true ties unlikely to be reported by any of the three, producing agreement on negative reports. Agreement on positive reports is informative under zero false positives, but agreement on negative reports is not verification that the dyads are non-ties. The observed level of agreement alone does not quantify how many jointly missed ties there are.
Why is that especially relevant for a one-hop exposure distribution rather than just the overall number of ties?

A one-hop exposure depends on the direct ties around individuals and treatment among those neighbors. Latent degree-related reporting could affect how many ties are missed around the same individual, not merely the total number of missed dyads. Even an accurate overall tie frequency would not necessarily tell us how ties are arranged across egos, and different arrangements can imply different one-hop exposures.
Suppose we could estimate a reporter’s marginal detection rate in each treatment stratum. Would that settle it?

Not necessarily. A marginal detection rate does not describe how detection by one reporter relates to detection by the others within groups sharing unobserved degree characteristics. Nor does it alone determine which true ties occur together around each individual. The exposure-identification argument would need the joint reporting behavior and enough information about the relevant neighborhood structure.
Is there a precise way to decide whether this is an identification failure rather than merely a poor estimate?

The identification test is whether two admissible accounts of true ties and reporter behavior can generate the same observable three-reporter patterns within treatment strata while implying different one-hop exposure distributions. If they can, those observations and restrictions do not point-identify the distribution. If the stated restrictions rule out such ambiguity, identification may still be possible. Estimation accuracy and interval width are separate questions.
Are you saying such observationally equivalent accounts have already been constructed for these three reporters?

No. That is what a nonidentification argument would need to demonstrate. The question raises latent degree-driven dependence as a potential obstacle; it supplies neither a specific reporter model nor a constructed pair of observationally equivalent accounts. We should not turn a plausible concern into a completed counterexample.
Could treatment stratification ever help with the latent-degree issue?

It can prevent treatment-related changes in reporting from being mistaken for a single common reporting pattern. But if reporters also share dependence driven by unobserved degree *within* each treatment stratum, stratification by treatment alone does not remove it. The two sources of variation need to be distinguished rather than treating control of one as control of both.
If we measured degree and conditioned on it, would the original reasoning automatically work?

Not automatically. We would need to know what degree measure is available when ties are incompletely reported and check whether conditioning on it actually yields the required independence. Other sources of shared reporting behavior could remain, and the resulting information would still need to identify the joint neighborhoods relevant to one-hop exposure. Measuring a variable called degree would be a possible ingredient, not a complete argument by itself.
Could the three reporters be independent for one dyad but still have reports correlated across dyads sharing an ego?

Yes. Independence across the three reporters for a particular dyad and independence across different dyads are distinct properties. Shared ego characteristics, including degree-related reporting, can induce dependence among reports for dyads around the same person. Because one-hop exposures involve whole direct neighborhoods, the identification argument should be explicit about which kind of independence it needs.
How would a bootstrap interact with this concern?

A bootstrap can characterize sampling variation for a specified estimator under an appropriate resampling scheme. It cannot recover an exposure distribution that the observed reports and assumptions do not identify. If latent degree-driven dependence invalidates the reporting model used to reconstruct exposures, bootstrapping the resulting policy g-computation will not, by itself, repair that identification problem.
Could a wider bootstrap interval compensate for unidentified exposures?

Not simply by being wider. An ordinary interval around a point estimate presumes an interpretable target and a justified estimation procedure. If multiple exposure distributions remain compatible with the same reports, their implications must be addressed through additional restrictions, information, or an explicit partial-identification analysis. The numerical width target for intervals in identifiable regimes does not make an unidentified distribution identifiable.
What can we conclude about population treatment-policy effects from reporter agreement alone?

We cannot conclude that the necessary one-hop exposure distributions—and hence the population treatment-policy effects calculated from them—are identified solely because three reporters agree within treatment strata. Zero false positives makes positive reports informative, but the all-negative patterns and neighborhood structure still matter. The effect also requires the other conditions for policy g-computation; exposure recovery is only one component.
Does the question call for dropping the three-reporter route altogether?

No such decision follows from the question. It asks whether latent degree-driven reporter dependence defeats the exposure-identification claim despite treatment-stratified agreement. The answer must be conditional on the reporting restrictions: check whether the required conditional independence actually holds or whether some other justified information resolves the dependence, and, if not, whether observationally equivalent processes yield different exposures.
And we cannot use the interval targets to decide that conditional-independence question?

Correct. The targets—at least 93% coverage for 95% intervals and median width no more than 2× the complete-network oracle’s in identifiable regimes—concern interval performance. They do not verify conditional independence or identify exposures. Those properties must be established on their own before interpreting interval performance as inference for the intended population policy effect.
So what is the narrow answer to my question?

Latent degree-driven dependence can invalidate an exposure-identification argument that assumes conditional independence of the three tie reporters, even when their treatment-stratified reports agree. It does not automatically prove nonidentification: that depends on the precise restrictions and whether the observable reports can distinguish exposure distributions. Agreement alone is not the needed identification test.

I want to sharpen the concern into a hypothesis: latent degree-driven dependence among tie reporters permits observationally equivalent tie distributions whose population treatment-policy effects differ by at least 0.05. If so, three-reporter identification would fail.

That is a proposed nonidentification argument, not a constructed counterexample yet. It calls for two admissible underlying tie distributions and reporting processes that produce the same observable information, despite differing in ways that make their population treatment-policy effects at least 0.05 apart. If such a pair can be established under the restrictions being examined, the observed three-reporter information cannot identify a unique value of that effect.
What must be observationally equivalent: just the overall number of reported ties?

No. Matching a total count would be too weak. The proposed pair must agree on the observable information available to the three-reporter analysis, including the relevant patterns of reports within treatment strata. If treatment and outcomes are also observed and used to infer the policy effect, their observable information must agree as well. The models would differ in what remains latent, not in something the analyst could already use to tell them apart.
What role does latent degree play in allowing that equivalence?

The hypothesis is that unobserved degree-related characteristics influence multiple reporters, creating shared detection patterns that cannot be explained by treating their reports as conditionally independent under the proposed observable conditioning. Different accounts of true ties and joint reporting behavior might then fit the same report patterns. That is the proposed mechanism; the hypothesis does not specify its probabilities or show that a particular pair of accounts has been constructed.
Could treatment stratification still leave that shared dependence in place?

Yes, as a possibility. Stratifying by treatment addresses differences across treatment strata, but latent degree-driven dependence could remain among the reporters within each stratum. The hypothesis asks whether that remaining flexibility allows the same observed three-reporter information to correspond to different underlying tie distributions and different policy effects.
Does agreement among three reporters rule out the hypothesis?

No. Agreement is an observable pattern, whereas the proposed shared dependence concerns why reporters agree or jointly miss ties. The hypothesis specifically allows observationally equivalent explanations despite treatment-stratified three-reporter information. To rule it out, one would need restrictions or information that distinguish the competing latent explanations, not agreement alone.
Do the reporters have to disagree often for the hypothesis to work?

No particular level of agreement or disagreement is specified. The proposed failure arises if distinct admissible tie and reporting processes yield the same observable reporter patterns, whatever those patterns are. Predicting how often reporters disagree would add an unprovided feature of the proposed counterexample.
How does zero false positives interact with this idea?

In the three-reporter proposal, zero false positives makes positive reports informative about true ties. It does not make a triple-negative report a verified non-tie. A degree-related propensity for reporters to miss the same true ties could leave ambiguity among triple-negative dyads even if no reporter ever invents a tie. Whether that ambiguity suffices for the claimed ≥0.05 difference still needs a construction.
Would two different rates of missed ties be enough to show the hypothesis?

Not by themselves. The rates would have to arise from admissible processes yielding the same full observable information, and the resulting underlying tie distributions would have to imply population treatment-policy effects that differ by at least 0.05. Different latent rates without observational equivalence, or without a difference in the target effect, would not demonstrate the stated claim.
Why specify a difference of at least 0.05 rather than merely two different effects?

It makes the hypothesis quantitatively specific: the two compatible effect values must be separated by ≥0.05 on the effect’s scale. Any nonzero difference would be relevant to a point-identification argument, but this hypothesis demands that particular minimum separation. No outcome unit, effect value, or practical interpretation of 0.05 is supplied.
Can we call that five percentage points?

Not without knowing that the policy effect is measured on a percentage or probability scale. The supplied hypothesis says only that the effects differ by at least 0.05. Reexpressing it as five percentage points would assume a scale that has not been stated.
Does ≥0.05 mean one policy effect must be positive and the other negative?

No. It constrains the separation between the effects, not their signs or individual values. They could differ by at least 0.05 without lying on opposite sides of zero. The hypothesis supplies no pair of numerical effect estimates.
Could identical observed tie reports still correspond to different one-hop exposures?

That is a possible route for the proposed argument. A one-hop exposure depends on true direct ties and treatment, not solely on which ties each reporter mentions. If latent degree-related joint omissions leave different true neighborhoods compatible with the same reports, policy-relevant exposures might differ. The hypothesis would have to show that this ambiguity leads to the required difference in population treatment-policy effects, rather than stopping at different networks.
Is a difference in overall tie prevalence enough to establish different one-hop exposure distributions?

It might matter, but the target can depend on how ties are arranged around individuals as well as how many ties there are overall. A rigorous counterexample should connect its latent tie distributions to the exposures and policy effects it claims differ. A tie-prevalence difference alone is not a substitute for that connection.
What exactly would ‘defeating three-reporter identification’ mean if the hypothesis is established?

It would mean that, when the stated latent degree-driven reporter dependence is allowed, the three-reporter observable information does not uniquely determine the population treatment-policy effect in the constructed setting. Two observationally equivalent admissible models would give effect values separated by ≥0.05. That conclusion would apply to the assumptions admitting those models; it would not mean that three reports can never identify an effect under more restrictive, justified conditions.
Are we already claiming that the conditional-independence restriction is false for the reporters?

No observed violation is reported here. The hypothesis examines what happens if latent degree-driven dependence is permitted and the independence needed for the three-reporter recovery is not justified under the relevant conditioning. A completed argument would need to say precisely which independence claim is at issue and show that its proposed models satisfy the conditions retained for the counterexample.
Could reporters be independent after conditioning on true degree while their treatment-stratified reports look dependent?

Conceptually, yes. Dependence can arise when reports are considered within treatment strata but an influential degree characteristic remains latent. That possibility illustrates why the conditioning set matters; it does not supply the observationally equivalent models or demonstrate the ≥0.05 policy-effect separation.
Does the hypothesis require each model to have the same actual true tie distribution?

No. It proposes observationally equivalent *tie distributions*: distinct underlying possibilities that cannot be distinguished from the available observed data. Requiring identical true tie distributions would remove the proposed latent ambiguity. The models must agree on observables while differing in their latent accounts and in the resulting policy effect by at least 0.05.
Could two models have different latent ties but the same population policy effect?

Yes, in principle, and such a pair would not establish this hypothesis. Nonidentification of latent network features does not automatically imply nonidentification of a particular policy effect. The proposed construction specifically requires different population treatment-policy effects, with the stated ≥0.05 separation.
Is it enough for the models to agree only on positive reports because zero false positives makes those reliable?

No. The all-negative and partially positive three-reporter patterns are also observable. Matching only the positive ties common to both models would leave open the possibility that other reporter patterns distinguish them. The observational-equivalence requirement must cover the information the analysis actually observes and uses.
Would observed outcomes have to be matched even if the underlying effects differ?

Yes, if those outcomes are part of the data used to claim identification of the population treatment-policy effect. The proposed difference could concern how the models imply outcomes under the policy while agreeing on observed information. The hypothesis does not provide an outcome model or a construction showing that this can be done, so we should not assert the matching has already been achieved.
Does this hypothesis itself tell us the identified range for the policy effect?

No. If a pair of observationally equivalent models with effects ≥0.05 apart were constructed, it would demonstrate at least that much ambiguity between two possible values under the stated restrictions. It would not, without further analysis, establish sharp lower and upper bounds or the full set of compatible effects. At present, even that pair remains hypothetical.
Could a bootstrap around three-reporter g-computation resolve the ambiguity?

Not if the ambiguity is genuine nonidentification. A bootstrap can reflect sampling variation for an analysis, but it cannot distinguish two models that imply the same distribution of observed information and different policy effects. The hypothesis concerns what the data can identify before interval performance is assessed.
Then is the ≥0.05 difference an interval-width result?

No. It is the hypothesized separation between population treatment-policy effects under observationally equivalent underlying models. It is not an oracle-width ratio, a coverage percentage, or the width of a confidence interval.
How should we evaluate this hypothesis without assuming the counterexample exists?

A valid evaluation would specify two admissible latent tie and reporter processes with degree-driven dependence, check that they generate the same observable information within the relevant treatment strata, and calculate the corresponding population treatment-policy effects. The key quantitative check is whether the effects differ by ≥0.05. Those are requirements for a demonstration, not steps already completed in the supplied hypothesis.
What if no such pair can be found under a precisely specified reporter model?

A failed attempt alone would not settle the question. One would need an argument that the model’s restrictions exclude observationally equivalent alternatives with different effects, or a valid construction showing that they do not. The current node offers a hypothesis about what latent degree-driven dependence permits; it reports neither a successful construction nor a proof ruling one out.
Does this require abandoning all uses of three reporters?

No such decision is part of the hypothesis. It challenges identification when latent degree-driven reporter dependence is allowed, despite treatment-stratified agreement. Different, adequately justified restrictions or additional information could change what is identifiable. We should not turn the proposed counterexample into a blanket verdict on every three-reporter analysis.
Can we phrase the hypothesis precisely in one sentence?

The hypothesis is that, when tie reporters share latent degree-driven dependence, two underlying tie distributions can be observationally equivalent under the treatment-stratified three-reporter information yet imply population treatment-policy effects differing by ≥0.05, so that those reports do not point-identify the effect under that permitted dependence.
Let’s construct observationally equivalent, degree-dependent three-reporter models and test whether their one-hop population treatment-policy effects differ by at least 0.05.

That activity directly tests the proposed nonidentification mechanism. The construction needs distinct underlying accounts of ties and degree-dependent reporting that agree on the information observable from the three reporters, while allowing their one-hop policy effects to be calculated separately. The decisive quantitative check is whether those effects differ by ≥0.05. No such pair or difference is reported yet.
What should we verify before comparing the policy effects?

First, that both models meet the restrictions being examined and generate the same relevant observable information. That includes the three-reporter patterns within treatment strata, rather than just an overall count of reported ties. If the policy-effect analysis also uses observed treatments and outcomes, observational equivalence must cover the relevant information from those observations too. Only then would a difference between the implied policy effects demonstrate ambiguity that the observed data cannot resolve.
Could we use two models that match the number of ties reported by each source but disagree on which dyads they report?

Matching three marginal totals would not ordinarily be enough. The identities and joint patterns of reports can be observable and informative: which reporters agree on a dyad, which disagree, and how those patterns vary by treatment stratum matter to the proposed analysis. The models need to match the observable information available to distinguish them, not merely a few summaries of it.
Does observational equivalence require the two models to have the same true ties?

No. The point of the proposed construction is that their latent tie distributions may differ while their observable implications agree. If the true network were observed completely, that latent ambiguity would disappear. What needs to be the same is the information the three-reporter analysis actually receives.
Where should degree enter the models?

The activity specifies degree-dependent three-reporter models, motivated by the possibility that latent degree drives shared reporting behavior. A construction would need to make that dependence explicit enough to check its implications for the observable report patterns and for true one-hop neighborhoods. It does not specify a distribution of degrees, a direction of degree dependence, or numerical reporting probabilities, so none of those can be presumed here.
Must higher-degree people be harder for all three reporters to observe?

No direction is stated. The proposed dependence could not be narrowed to lower or higher detection at higher degrees without adding a model detail. What matters for the test is whether admissible degree-driven reporting can make distinct underlying tie structures observationally equivalent while their one-hop policy effects differ by the required amount.
Why specifically three reporters, rather than just comparing two incomplete networks?

The construction is meant to test the three-reporter recovery route. It must show whether all three observable reporting sources, considered together within the relevant treatment strata, still leave the proposed ambiguity when degree-driven dependence is permitted. Comparing only two reports would not directly answer that question.
Does the construction have to preserve the zero-false-positive restriction from that route?

To test whether latent dependence defeats the proposed three-reporter approach while its other reporting restrictions remain in force, the candidate models would need to respect those retained restrictions, including zero false positives. Then positive reports would still indicate true ties, while jointly missed true ties could remain possible. If a construction instead used false positives, it would test a different departure and would not isolate the degree-dependence concern.
How can zero false positives coexist with different latent tie distributions that have the same observed reports?

Zero false positives constrains what a positive report can mean; it does not establish that every true tie appears in a report. Conceptually, ambiguity can remain among dyads with no positive reports. Whether two different allocations of such latent ties can reproduce the same full three-reporter observations and change the policy effect by ≥0.05 is exactly what the construction must establish, not something we can infer merely from that possibility.
Should treatment stratification be held fixed between the models?

The observational comparison must respect the treatment information used in the three-reporter analysis. In particular, the models need to agree on the observable reporter patterns within the relevant treatment strata. Otherwise treatment-stratified data could distinguish them, and they would not furnish the proposed counterexample.
Is it enough to show that the models give different one-hop exposure distributions?

Not for the stated quantitative test. Different exposures would help explain a route by which the policy effects might differ, but the activity specifically asks whether the *one-hop policy effects* differ by at least 0.05. Two different exposure distributions could still imply the same policy effect. That final target comparison cannot be skipped.
Do the models need to imply different outcomes among the people we actually observe?

If observed outcomes form part of the information used for the policy analysis, the models must agree on their observable distribution to be observationally equivalent. Their implied outcomes under a policy, and hence their policy effects, could nonetheless differ if the latent structure leaves that implication unresolved. The activity does not supply an outcome model or an achieved matching construction, so this remains a requirement to check rather than a reported fact.
Should we choose a particular treatment policy now to make the ≥0.05 comparison concrete?

A concrete calculation would need a well-defined policy effect, but this activity does not name a policy or contrast. We can state what the comparison must show without inventing one: the same population treatment-policy target, evaluated under each admissible model, must take values separated by ≥0.05. Comparing different targets across the two models would not establish nonidentification of a single effect.
Can the two effect values differ by 0.05 without having opposite signs?

Yes. The threshold concerns their separation, not their signs. The activity specifies neither individual effect value nor an outcome scale, so we should report the threshold as ≥0.05 rather than assigning example effect values or converting it to percentage points.
Would a difference smaller than 0.05 still matter?

Any genuine difference between effects under observationally equivalent admissible models would matter for point identification. But this activity tests the sharper hypothesis that the separation reaches at least 0.05. A smaller difference would not meet that numerical test, and we cannot say in advance whether a pair with a larger difference exists.
Could we claim success if we find two different networks but cannot show their reports are observationally equivalent?

No. If the observed three-reporter information distinguishes the models, the data could in principle distinguish their implications. Distinct true networks alone do not establish the intended nonidentification argument. Both observational equivalence and the ≥0.05 policy-effect separation are essential checks.
And what if they are observationally equivalent but their policy effects coincide?

That pair would demonstrate ambiguity about some latent features, but not the claimed ambiguity about this policy effect. The activity must test the target itself. An effect can remain identifiable even when every underlying tie is not individually identified, so a difference in latent tie distributions is not enough.
Are we testing the conditional-independence proposal under its own assumptions, or what happens when latent degree dependence is allowed?

The activity examines the latter: whether permitting degree-driven dependence among the three reporters leaves observationally equivalent models with different one-hop policy effects. It should be clear which restrictions are retained and which reporter-independence restriction is being challenged. A counterexample under permitted dependence would establish a boundary for the three-reporter route under that relaxation; it would not, by itself, refute an identification result that explicitly and correctly assumes the relevant conditional independence.
Could the reporters be independent after conditioning on latent degree and still have the dependence we are worried about?

Conceptually, yes. Reports can be dependent under a coarser observed conditioning set if they share an unobserved degree-related factor, even when a richer hypothetical conditioning set would remove that dependence. The construction must specify enough of the joint reporting behavior to verify observational equivalence. The activity does not say that any particular conditional-independence formulation has already been shown to hold or fail.
Would a bootstrap of the three-reporter policy estimates settle which model is right?

Not if the constructed models really are observationally equivalent. Resampling the same kind of observable information would not distinguish two admissible models that imply identical observables but different policy effects. This activity tests identification before asking whether a bootstrap interval meets coverage or oracle-width targets.
If we construct the pair and the effect separation reaches 0.05, what is the properly scoped conclusion?

It would show that the specified three-reporter observable information does not point-identify the one-hop population treatment-policy effect when the degree-dependent reporting behavior admitted by those models is allowed. The two compatible effects would be at least 0.05 apart. It would not establish sharp bounds, identify every possible effect value, or rule out identification under stronger justified assumptions.
Does constructing a pair tell us the full width of a partially identified effect range?

No. A successful pair would demonstrate at least the separation between those two compatible values. Other compatible models might imply effects elsewhere, and determining the full or sharp identified set would require additional analysis. The activity asks for observationally equivalent models and the ≥0.05 comparison, not a bound calculation.
What if no pair meeting the threshold emerges from this construction attempt?

That would not automatically prove three-reporter identification or show that no such pair exists. It could mean the attempted construction did not find one, or that the chosen restrictions prevent this particular mechanism. A general identification conclusion would require an argument ruling out relevant observationally equivalent alternatives, not just an unsuccessful search.
So how should we state the work now, without implying the test has already succeeded?

Construct two admissible degree-dependent three-reporter models, check that they are observationally equivalent on the relevant treatment-stratified information, and calculate the same one-hop population treatment-policy effect under each. Then test whether the effects differ by ≥0.05. Those are the checks to perform; neither observational equivalence nor the effect separation has yet been reported as a result.

The three-reporter analysis produced a different distinction than I expected: across all the latent-degree models examined under network-independent Bernoulli policies, the population treatment-policy effect gaps were zero. But zero-sensitivity treatment strata defeated three-reporter identification.

Those are separate findings. For the latent-degree models under network-independent Bernoulli policies, the compared policy effects had zero gaps. That does not say the underlying tie distributions were identical or that one-hop exposure distributions were identified. Separately, zero-sensitivity treatment strata prevented the three-reporter information from identifying what the proposed recovery required. Neither finding should be generalized beyond its stated conditions.
Does a zero effect gap mean the reporters recovered every missing tie?

No. A zero gap compares the population treatment-policy effects implied by the models examined. Different latent tie distributions can, in principle, imply the same effect for a particular class of policies. Equality of that target does not establish that every tie—or the full one-hop exposure distribution—was recovered.
Why does the policy class matter so much when stating the zero-gap result?

Because the finding is explicitly under network-independent Bernoulli policies. It says the effect gaps were zero for that policy class across the latent-degree models examined. It does not supply effect comparisons for policies that depend on the network or use a different assignment structure, so we cannot extend zero gaps to them.
Can we say latent degree-driven reporter dependence is harmless, then?

Not generally. The zero-gap finding is about a specified policy effect in the examined models. Latent degree-driven dependence could still matter for recovering ties or exposures, and the result does not establish performance for every policy. It is more precise to say that the examined latent-degree models did not produce differing effects under network-independent Bernoulli policies.
What is the distinction between an unidentified exposure distribution and an effect gap of zero?

Exposure identification asks whether the observed reports determine the distribution of relevant one-hop treatment exposures. Effect identification asks whether they determine the particular population policy effect. Even if multiple underlying exposure distributions remain possible, they might lead to the same value of a particular effect. A zero effect gap therefore cannot, by itself, settle the exposure-identification question.
Does ‘across all latent-degree models’ establish a result for every degree-dependent reporting process someone might devise?

It should be read with the scope of the finding: all latent-degree models covered by this analysis, under network-independent Bernoulli policies. The statement does not define a universal class of every conceivable degree-dependent reporter process. It also does not give model specifications that would justify enlarging that scope.
How should I interpret ‘zero-sensitivity treatment strata’?

Sensitivity concerns detecting a true tie. A zero-sensitivity treatment stratum supplies no positive detection of true ties through the reporting information whose sensitivity is zero in that stratum. The finding says such strata defeated three-reporter identification. It does not specify which treatment strata were affected or provide numerical sensitivities for other strata.
Does having three reporters overcome zero sensitivity just because there are three of them?

No. The number of reporters cannot create information about true ties in a stratum if the reporting signals needed to distinguish them have zero sensitivity there. The finding specifically identifies zero-sensitivity treatment strata as a failure point for three-reporter identification; treatment stratification alone does not remove that failure.
Is zero sensitivity the same as zero false positives?

No. Zero false positives means a non-tie is not falsely reported as a tie. Zero sensitivity means true ties are not detected by the reporting signal in the affected stratum. The original proposal’s zero-false-positive condition does not guarantee positive sensitivity, and these two zeros must not be conflated.
With zero false positives, couldn’t an absence of positive reports establish that a dyad is a non-tie?

No. Zero false positives tells us how to interpret a positive report; it does not make a negative report conclusive. In a zero-sensitivity stratum, true ties may fail to generate the positive reports needed to distinguish them from non-ties. That is why the absence of reported ties cannot simply be treated as verified absence of ties.
Does the zero-sensitivity finding identify particular alternative networks or quantify their effect difference?

Not in the stated evidence. It reports that zero-sensitivity treatment strata defeated three-reporter identification, without giving model constructions, particular networks, or an effect-gap magnitude for that failure. The zero effect gaps are reported for the latent-degree models under network-independent Bernoulli policies; we should not attach those gaps to an unspecified zero-sensitivity counterexample or invent a different gap for it.
So are the two findings logically contradictory: zero gaps, but failed identification?

No. They address different distinctions. Zero gaps concern the specified policy effects across the examined latent-degree models under network-independent Bernoulli policies. Zero-sensitivity strata concern a failure of the three-reporter identification route. The statements need not assert the same target, information conditions, or model comparison to coexist.
Could I say the three-reporter approach identifies one-hop exposures whenever the effect gaps happen to be zero?

No. Equal effects do not imply equal exposure distributions, and a numerical comparison among models does not by itself establish that reports determine the exposures. Exposure recovery needs its own identification argument. The zero-sensitivity result also cautions against claiming that three treatment-stratified reporters always provide enough information.
What does treatment stratification accomplish if a stratum has zero sensitivity?

It keeps reporting behavior in that stratum distinct from behavior in other treatment strata, which is useful for stating the limitation accurately. But separating strata does not give an uninformative stratum positive sensitivity. The finding concerns precisely a situation where a stratum-specific lack of detection defeats the proposed identification route.
Can information from other treatment strata automatically fill the gap?

Not from this evidence alone. Borrowing information across strata would require restrictions connecting their underlying ties or reporting processes. No such restriction or successful recovery is stated here, so information in other strata cannot simply be assumed to identify the zero-sensitivity stratum.
Does conditional independence among the three reporters repair zero sensitivity?

Conditional independence describes how their reports relate once the relevant conditions are fixed; it cannot, by itself, create detections of true ties where sensitivity is zero. The finding therefore exposes a limitation that a conditional-independence assumption alone does not resolve.
What can we conclude about bootstrap policy g-computation from these findings?

They do not report bootstrap interval coverage or width. A bootstrap cannot supply the missing tie information in a zero-sensitivity stratum simply by resampling reports. Conversely, the zero effect gaps under the specified Bernoulli policies are not an interval-performance result. Neither the ≥93% coverage target for 95% intervals nor the median-width limit of ≤2× the complete-network oracle is evaluated in this finding.
Should we regard a zero gap as proof of identification for every network-independent Bernoulli policy?

The supported statement is that effect gaps were zero across the latent-degree models examined under network-independent Bernoulli policies. To claim identification for an entire policy class, one would have to establish that all admissible observationally equivalent models covered by the identification question agree on the target. The brief result should not be expanded into that proof.
What is the sharpest way to report the result without collapsing the two parts?

Across the latent-degree models examined under network-independent Bernoulli policies, population treatment-policy effect gaps were zero. Zero-sensitivity treatment strata, however, defeated three-reporter identification. The first finding concerns equality of the specified policy effects in those model comparisons; the second identifies a limitation of recovering the needed information from the reporters.

Let’s reject unrestricted three-reporter inference because zero-sensitivity treatment strata defeat identification. I also want the decision to be clear that latent-degree dependence alone did not separate the effects under network-independent Bernoulli policies.

That states both the decision and its qualification. Three-reporter inference should not be used without restrictions that address zero-sensitivity treatment strata: in those strata, the reporter information does not support the claimed identification. The reason is not a demonstrated difference between the Bernoulli-policy effects in the latent-degree models; those effect gaps were zero.
What does “unrestricted” qualify here?

It qualifies the scope of the three-reporter inference being rejected. Having three treatment-stratified reporters is not, by itself, enough to claim identification when a treatment stratum can have zero sensitivity. The decision does not say that every possible three-reporter analysis is impossible under additional, justified restrictions.
Should I say we’re rejecting three reporters because latent degree caused different policy effects?

No. That would reverse an explicit part of the decision. Latent-degree dependence alone did not separate the effects under the network-independent Bernoulli policies considered. The stated reason for rejecting *unrestricted* three-reporter inference is that zero-sensitivity treatment strata defeat identification.
Is zero sensitivity a problem even if reports are separated by treatment stratum?

Yes. Stratification makes the reporting conditions visible separately for each treatment stratum, but it cannot create tie detections in a stratum where sensitivity is zero. The decision treats that lack of identifying information as a boundary for an unrestricted claim based on the three reporters.
Does this mean zero sensitivity is the same as allowing false positive reports?

No. Sensitivity concerns detection of true ties; false positives concern reports of ties that are not truly present. The decision concerns zero-sensitivity treatment strata. A restriction against false positives does not, on its own, ensure positive sensitivity in every relevant treatment stratum.
If a stratum has zero sensitivity, can three negative reports establish that its dyads are non-ties?

Not on that basis. When true ties can produce no positive detection in an affected stratum, negative reports do not distinguish true ties from non-ties there. That is why simply adding reporters does not support an unrestricted identification claim in the setting named by the decision.
Do we have to specify which treatment stratum has zero sensitivity to state the decision?

No particular stratum is named here. The decision is that permitting zero-sensitivity treatment strata defeats unrestricted three-reporter identification. We should not invent which treatments define an affected stratum or assign sensitivities to the others.
Could you explain the latent-degree qualification without making it sound like a guarantee?

The qualification is narrow: latent-degree dependence alone did not yield different population treatment-policy effects across the models examined under network-independent Bernoulli policies. That does not guarantee that tie distributions, one-hop exposures, or effects under other policy classes agree. It also does not remove the separate identification obstacle posed by zero-sensitivity strata.
So a zero effect gap is not the same thing as saying the reporters identify every true tie?

Correct. Two underlying accounts can agree on a particular policy effect without revealing every true tie. The decision distinguishes equality of the Bernoulli-policy effects in the latent-degree comparisons from the broader question of whether three reports identify the network information required for inference.
Does rejecting unrestricted inference imply that the Bernoulli-policy effects were shown to be different under zero sensitivity?

No numerical difference under zero-sensitivity strata is stated in this decision. It says those strata defeat identification, while latent-degree dependence alone did not separate effects under network-independent Bernoulli policies. We should not transfer the zero-gap finding to a different comparison or invent an effect gap for the zero-sensitivity case.
Can we say the three-reporter approach is rejected for every network-independent Bernoulli policy?

That is broader than the decision. What is rejected is *unrestricted* three-reporter inference because zero-sensitivity treatment strata can defeat identification. Separately, the examined latent-degree dependence alone did not separate Bernoulli-policy effects. Neither statement is a blanket ruling that all inference for that policy class fails.
And can we say latent degree-driven dependence never threatens identification?

No. The decision reports only that it did not, by itself, produce separated effects under the specified network-independent Bernoulli policies. It does not settle what other policy targets or reporting conditions would imply. The reason given for this particular rejection remains zero-sensitivity treatment strata.
How does this affect the idea of bootstrapping policy g-computation from the three reports?

A bootstrap can address uncertainty in an analysis whose target and required inputs are identified under its assumptions. It cannot make an unrestricted three-reporter identification claim valid when zero-sensitivity strata leave needed information unresolved. This decision does not evaluate a bootstrap’s coverage or oracle-relative width under additional restrictions.
Is the decision about poor interval coverage?

No. Its reason is an identification failure when zero-sensitivity treatment strata are allowed. It gives no three-reporter interval coverage percentage or width ratio. Rejecting unrestricted identification should not be restated as though a numerical interval-performance target had been tested and missed.
Does this decide whether useful bounds could still be reported when a stratum has zero sensitivity?

No. Rejecting an unrestricted point-identification claim does not, by itself, specify whether informative bounds can be obtained, what assumptions they would require, or how wide they would be. The decision concerns the scope of three-reporter inference, not a completed bounds analysis.
What would we need to keep separate when communicating this decision?

Keep three things distinct: the unrestricted identification claim that is rejected, the zero-sensitivity treatment strata that motivate that rejection, and the zero effect gaps observed for latent-degree models under network-independent Bernoulli policies. Equal effects in that limited comparison neither repair zero sensitivity nor demonstrate that latent-degree dependence produced the claimed identification failure.
Can you put the decision in one sentence without losing that distinction?

Reject unrestricted three-reporter inference because zero-sensitivity treatment strata defeat identification, while noting that latent-degree dependence alone did not separate population treatment-policy effects under network-independent Bernoulli policies.

I’d like to consider a design that compares policies directly. Randomize isolated clusters 1:1 between a Bernoulli(0.3) treatment policy and a Bernoulli(0.7) treatment policy, then use a contrast of cluster-mean outcomes regardless of treatment-dependent tie reporting.

That is a proposal to estimate the population effect of assigning clusters to those two policies without reconstructing the social network. The 1:1 randomization allocates clusters between the policy arms; Bernoulli(0.3) and Bernoulli(0.7) describe the treatment policies within those arms. With clusters isolated for interference, a contrast of their observed mean outcomes could target the difference between the two policy regimes even if treatment changes which ties are reported. This is a proposed design and identification route, not a reported result or interval-performance finding.
Why doesn’t treatment-dependent tie reporting necessarily prevent that contrast?

Because the proposed contrast uses cluster-mean outcomes under randomized policy assignment, not a reconstructed set of ties or individual one-hop exposures. If the outcome information needed to calculate those cluster means is available, changes in which ties are reported need not enter the calculation. That does not make the reports accurate; it makes them unnecessary for this particular contrast under the proposal’s conditions.
Does ‘regardless of treatment-dependent tie reporting’ mean we can ignore all forms of missing data?

No. It refers specifically to reporting of social ties. It does not say outcomes are always observed or that missing outcomes can be ignored. If outcome availability or cluster membership were affected in a way that changes the measured cluster means, that would raise a different issue not resolved simply by avoiding reported ties.
Can you separate the 1:1 and the 0.3 and 0.7 numbers?

The 1:1 ratio concerns randomization of isolated clusters to one of two policy arms. The 0.3 and 0.7 are the Bernoulli treatment probabilities defining the policies being compared. They are not percentages of clusters assigned to each arm, coverage values, census fractions, or probabilities that ties are reported.
So does Bernoulli(0.3) mean that exactly 30% of people in every cluster receive treatment?

No. A Bernoulli(0.3) policy assigns treatment with probability 0.3; it does not fix the realized treated fraction at exactly 30% in every cluster. Likewise, Bernoulli(0.7) does not require exactly 70% treated in each cluster. The policy contrast concerns the outcome distributions induced by the two assignment regimes, not fixed realized proportions.
Does the 1:1 allocation mean every person has a one-half treatment probability?

No. One-half is the proposed chance that a cluster is assigned to each policy arm. Within a cluster, treatment follows the policy to which that cluster is assigned: Bernoulli(0.3) or Bernoulli(0.7). Treating the cluster-level arm assignment as an individual treatment probability would conflate two different randomizations.
What exactly is being contrasted if outcomes can reflect interference?

The comparison is between cluster-mean outcomes under the Bernoulli(0.3) and Bernoulli(0.7) policies. A cluster’s mean can reflect the effects of the treatment configuration generated by its policy, including spillovers among members, rather than isolating each person’s own-treatment effect. The proposal does not specify a policy-effect scale beyond the contrast of cluster means or fix which policy’s mean is subtracted from the other.
Do we need to recover one-hop exposure distributions for this estimand?

Not for the proposed direct comparison of randomized policy arms. The design observes how cluster-mean outcomes differ when clusters receive the two policies, rather than calculating outcomes under those policies from estimated one-hop exposures. That is why treatment-dependent tie reporting can be beside the point for this specified policy contrast. It would not follow that one-hop exposure distributions themselves are identified.
Could the comparison still include effects that pass through unreported social ties?

Yes, within an isolated cluster, its observed outcome mean can reflect consequences of treatment that pass through underlying ties whether or not those ties were reported. The method compares outcomes generated by policy assignment; it does not need to label each pathway to include it in that policy contrast. This is not a claim that unreported ties are recovered or that their separate effects can be estimated.
What does cluster isolation contribute?

It limits interference across policy arms at the cluster boundary. If a cluster’s outcomes can depend on treatment assigned in another cluster, its mean may not represent only the policy assigned to its own cluster. Isolation is therefore a substantive condition for interpreting a between-cluster policy contrast, not just a convenient label for the sampling units.
Does isolated mean there cannot be interference among people within a cluster?

No. Isolation concerns cross-cluster spillovers. The proposal is motivated by network interference, and the cluster-mean outcome may include within-cluster consequences of the assigned policy. It does not require us to assume that one person’s treatment affects only that person, though the proposal also does not specify a particular within-cluster interference mechanism.
Could the policy contrast remain interpretable if social ties between clusters are reported inconsistently?

The decisive issue is whether clusters are isolated for interference, not merely whether cross-cluster ties are reported. Inconsistent tie reports do not establish isolation, and unreported connections that transmit treatment effects could violate it. The claim that tie reporting need not be used to calculate the contrast is conditional on genuine isolation; it is not a way to dismiss cross-cluster spillovers.
Do we need to identify the true network to know that clusters are isolated?

The proposal takes isolated clusters as a condition. It does not specify how that condition is established, and avoiding tie information in the outcome contrast does not prove isolation. Any identification claim should make the isolation assumption visible rather than infer it from incomplete reports of ties.
Does this design identify an effect for any treatment policy I might later choose?

No. Its direct randomized comparison is between the two stated regimes, Bernoulli(0.3) and Bernoulli(0.7). Estimating the effect of another policy, or a network-adaptive policy, would be a different question. A contrast between these two arms should not be treated as identifying every population treatment-policy effect.
Would it tell us which particular tie carried an effect?

No. Cluster-mean contrasts can compare the overall outcomes under the two policies without attributing effects to individual ties, reporters, or exposure categories. That is both the attraction and the limitation of this route: it avoids relying on treatment-dependent tie reports for this policy contrast, but does not resolve detailed network mechanisms.
If each cluster has a mean outcome, can we treat every individual outcome as an independent replicate for inference?

Not just because individual outcomes are observed. Policy assignment is at the cluster level, and outcomes within a cluster can be dependent under interference. The proposal specifies cluster-mean contrasts, which keeps the cluster as the comparison unit. It does not specify an interval estimator or license an individual-level independence assumption.
Do cluster means automatically give equal weight to every person in the population?

That depends on how cluster means are aggregated and on the population target. The proposal says to use cluster-mean contrasts but does not specify cluster sizes, population weighting, or whether the target is an equally weighted cluster mean versus an individual-weighted population mean. Those definitions would need to align before claiming that a particular numerical contrast identifies a particular population effect.
Could we at least say randomization helps distinguish policy assignment from preexisting network differences?

Yes, as the rationale for the proposal. Randomizing isolated clusters 1:1 assigns which policy each cluster receives rather than selecting arms according to their recorded ties. That supports a direct policy comparison under the design’s conditions. It does not, by itself, ensure the clusters are isolated, outcomes are measured appropriately, or that a proposed confidence interval attains a specified performance target.
What if treatment influences which ties we see more strongly under Bernoulli(0.7) than Bernoulli(0.3)?

Differences in tie reporting between the policy arms do not by themselves alter the definition of a contrast based on cluster-mean outcomes, provided those means are measured comparably and the isolation condition holds. We should still avoid interpreting the reported networks as comparable complete descriptions of exposure. The proposal’s claim is about estimating this policy contrast without using tie reports, not about eliminating differences in reporting.
Would analyzing only clusters with certain reported ties undermine the appeal of the design?

It could. Selecting clusters for the outcome contrast according to treatment-dependent reported ties would introduce those reports into an analysis that is proposed to avoid depending on them. The proposal calls for a cluster-mean contrast under randomized policy assignment; it does not include such a tie-based selection rule.
Does the proposal already specify what kind of interval to use?

No. It specifies randomization of isolated clusters between the two Bernoulli policies and a cluster-mean contrast. It gives no bootstrap, randomization-based interval, or other interval procedure, and no coverage or oracle-width result. Those details should not be added as if they were part of the proposal.
How do the broader interval targets apply to this route?

If this policy contrast is identified under the proposed conditions, its 95% intervals would still need at least 93% coverage and median width no more than 2× the complete-network oracle’s to meet the stated performance goal. Neither cluster randomization nor avoiding reported ties establishes those numerical properties by itself.
Could a complete-network oracle make the two policies into a different estimand?

The oracle is a benchmark for interval width, not a reason to change the policy contrast. A meaningful width comparison would target the same effect of Bernoulli(0.3) versus Bernoulli(0.7), while allowing the oracle its complete-network information. The proposal does not report an oracle interval or specify how it would be constructed.
Is it accurate to say this proposal solves all treatment-dependent missing-tie problems?

No. It proposes a way to make *this direct policy contrast* independent of tie-reporting information when the required cluster outcomes are measured and interference is confined to isolated clusters. It does not identify missing ties, recover exposure distributions, or cover effects for policies not randomized in the design.
Please state the proposal concisely while keeping its restrictions and the two policies explicit.

Randomize isolated clusters 1:1 between Bernoulli(0.3) and Bernoulli(0.7) treatment policies, and compare their cluster-mean outcomes to estimate that population policy contrast without relying on treatment-dependent reports of social ties. Identification and interval performance remain conditional on the design and measurement requirements; neither is reported as established by this proposal alone.
With unequal cluster sizes, does the unweighted cluster-mean contrast identify a cluster-average rather than the population individual-average policy effect?

Generally, yes. An unweighted contrast gives each cluster mean the same weight, so its natural target is the average policy contrast across clusters. A population individual-average effect instead gives each person equal weight, which means larger clusters contribute more. With unequal cluster sizes, those targets need not coincide. The precise conclusion still depends on how the population, cluster selection, and policy contrast are defined.
Can you explain the distinction without assuming any particular cluster sizes?

Imagine calculating a mean outcome for each cluster under each policy. Averaging those cluster means equally answers, in effect, what the average cluster-level mean is under each policy. To average over individuals, each cluster mean must contribute in proportion to the number of people it represents. If cluster sizes differ, equal cluster weights and equal person weights are different operations.
Does the 1:1 randomization between Bernoulli(0.3) and Bernoulli(0.7) decide which of those two averages is identified?

No. The 1:1 allocation says how clusters are assigned to the two policy arms. It does not specify whether the population estimand weights clusters equally or people equally. The Bernoulli(0.3) and Bernoulli(0.7) policies define the regimes being compared; weighting determines whose outcomes are emphasized in the resulting population contrast.
So random assignment of policies can be sound while the contrast targets the wrong population average?

Yes, if the intended target is an individual-average effect but the analysis uses equal cluster weights without justification. Randomization helps compare outcomes under the assigned policies; it does not automatically equate a cluster-average estimand with an individual-average one. Calling one the other would be a target-definition error, not evidence that randomization failed.
Could you write the two targets conceptually?

Let a cluster’s policy contrast be the difference between its mean outcome under Bernoulli(0.7) and its mean outcome under Bernoulli(0.3), using that subtraction order only for illustration. A cluster-average effect averages those cluster contrasts with equal weight per cluster. An individual-average effect averages them with weight proportional to cluster size, assuming the population consists of the people in those clusters. The question does not fix a subtraction order; reversing it reverses the sign of both targets without changing the weighting distinction.
Does interference inside a cluster change that basic weighting distinction?

No. Interference affects what an outcome under a policy means: it may depend on treatment assigned to other members of the cluster. Once the two policy-specific cluster means are defined, however, an equal-weight average over clusters still differs from an individual-weighted average when cluster sizes vary. The weighting issue persists whether within-cluster interference is simple or complex.
Would different-sized clusters necessarily have different policy effects?

No. Unequal size makes the two averaging rules different, but it does not guarantee different numerical answers. If the cluster-specific policy contrasts happen to be the same, for example, either averaging rule yields that same contrast. The question is whether equality can be assumed; unequal sizes alone do not establish it.
Can they coincide even if cluster-specific effects are not identical?

They can, depending on how cluster sizes and cluster-specific contrasts relate. What matters is whether the equal-cluster-weight average and the size-weighted average happen to be equal. That can occur without identical contrasts, but it is not guaranteed by 1:1 policy randomization or by the existence of isolated clusters.
What if larger clusters tend to have different contrasts from smaller ones?

Then the distinction can be consequential. The individual-average effect places more weight on the larger clusters’ contrasts, while the unweighted cluster-average effect does not. This is a conditional illustration of the weighting issue, not an assertion that cluster size and policy response are related in the setting under discussion.
Does taking a mean within each cluster already give equal weight to all people?

It gives equal weight to people *within that cluster’s mean*. Averaging those means equally across clusters is a second step: a person in a smaller cluster then has more influence on the overall average than a person in a larger cluster. Equal weighting within clusters therefore does not imply equal weighting across all individuals.
What if I pool every individual outcome within each policy arm instead of averaging cluster means equally?

Pooling outcomes gives more weight to larger observed clusters and may align more closely with an individual-average target. But whether that pooled contrast identifies the specified *population* individual-average policy effect depends on the population being represented, the policy assignment design, and how the arm-specific totals are handled. Pooling changes the weighting; it is not automatically a complete identification argument.
Could I instead give each cluster mean a weight equal to its size?

Size-weighting cluster means is the direct conceptual route to an average over individuals when those clusters and their members define the population target. The weights would need to be applied consistently to the two policy-specific quantities. If clusters enter the observed analysis through a separate sampling process, that design would also matter; the current question supplies no such additional design details.
If we use cluster-size weights, are we changing the policies from Bernoulli(0.3) and Bernoulli(0.7)?

No. The policies remain the same. Cluster-size weights change how outcomes under the two policies are aggregated into a population effect. They do not change the treatment probabilities defining either policy.
Can an unweighted cluster-mean contrast ever be exactly the estimand we want?

Certainly, if the target is the average effect across clusters, giving each cluster equal importance. The concern arises only when that contrast is described as the population *individual-average* effect without a reason the two averages agree. Neither estimand is inherently the wrong one; the estimand and estimator have to match.
Does the word ‘population’ alone tell us whether the unit being averaged is a person or a cluster?

No. A population policy effect can be defined by averaging over clusters or over individuals. With unequal cluster sizes, it is important to say which population unit has equal weight. The phrase ‘population treatment-policy effect’ does not settle that choice by itself.
Could unequal sizes also affect the precision of an interval, apart from the estimand?
